content: A Las Vegas jury found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of murder for orchestrating the killing of rap legend Tupac Shakur, ending one of the country’s most notorious cold cases nearly 30 years later. After just three hours of deliberation, jurors convicted Davis, a former Los Angeles gang leader, of facilitating the 1996 drive-by shooting in Las Vegas that left the iconic rapper dead at the age of 25. The verdict came after a two-week trial in which prosecutors argued that Davis had ordered the killing in revenge for Tupac beating up his nephew – a case they made by citing the man’s own repeated public statements tying himself to the famous crime. Davis’ defense attorneys argued that those statements were essentially fictional, aimed at helping to boost his notoriety and sell books. But prosecutors told the jury Davis had told the truth in an effort to profit from his crime: “Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty.” Shakur, then a rising superstar in the rap world, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas in 1996. The shooting took place on Sept. 7, 1996; he died six days later. His death, which came amid the infamous East Coast-West Coast hip-hop feud, was followed months later by the shooting of rival The Notorious B.I.G. No one was charged with either killing, and the pair of cold cases became a fixture in American cultural history. But in September 2023, prosecutors unveiled a murder indictment against Davis, a former Crips gang leader in 1990s Los Angeles, claiming he’d orchestrated the killing as revenge after Shakur’s entourage beat up his nephew earlier that night. They cited his own words as evidence, including a 2019 tell-all memoir and podcast interviews in which he candidly described his role in the crime. Across two weeks of trial, prosecutors called 24 witnesses and played more than eight hours of recordings, mostly of Davis himself discussing his role in the killing. Defense attorney Michael Sanft presented only a brief defense, calling just three police investigators to testify about the killing and its aftermath. Following the conviction, Davis, 63, could be sentenced to life in prison without parole. The judge will weigh the potential sentence and hand down his decision at a later date.

content: Suno is facing yet another copyright infringement lawsuit, this time alleging its popular AI music model was trained on regional Mexican hits in order to generate Spanish-language songs. The legal complaint was filed Monday (Aug. 31) by Gerencia 360 Music, an independent regional Mexican record label and publisher. It’s the latest in a string of AI training lawsuits brought against Suno by music rightsholders, including the majors, indies and individual artists. Like other rightsholders, Gerencia alleges that Suno ripped its music from streaming services and then fed it into the training corpus for an AI model that now allows users to generate new songs with the click of a button. Monday’s lawsuit, however, specifically says Gerencia’s catalog was necessary for Suno to teach its model to create songs in Spanish. “Gerencia’s works are especially important to Suno because they are hugely popular Spanish language works, which Suno has misappropriated to train its models so they may provide Spanish language songs in response to user queries,” reads the complaint, filed by veteran music litigator Richard Busch. “Without its infringement of Gerencia’s Spanish language copyrighted works, Suno would not have been well-positioned to capture a significant share of the Spanish language AI user market.” Busch says Gerencia’s catalog includes “some of the most recognizable and commercially valuable songs in the history of Regional Mexican and Latin music,” including works by Adriel Favela, Javier Rosas, Giovanny Ayala, Cornelio Vega y su Dinastia and Noel Torres. The lawsuit is seeking nearly $100 million in damages. A Suno rep declined to comment on the lawsuit Monday. Suno’s copyright troubles began in 2024, when the three major labels banded together to sue the AI company for infringing their sound recordings “at an almost unimaginable scale.” Other rightsholders have since jumped in with their own copyright infringement suits against Suno, including a group of indie artists pursuing class action status and production music company Jamendo. Two weeks ago, indie publisher Round Hill Music opened up another case (also authored by Busch). Suno maintains that its AI training process was legal under copyright law’s fair use principle, which allows unlicensed works to be reused for transformative purposes. It remains to be seen whether a judge will agree; fair use is an untested legal question at the center of dozens of ongoing AI copyright lawsuits right now. Meanwhile, Suno has made peace with some big players in the music industry. Warner Music Group (WMG) exited the majors’ lawsuit last fall by inking a landmark settlement that requires to Suno to train a new model on licensed music, and BMG reached a similar deal with Suno earlier this month.

content: A composer who worked on The Lion King’s iconic “Circle of Life” must now repay nearly $40,000 in legal bills after filing a failed lawsuit against a comedian who joked about the song on a podcast. Comedian Learnmore Jonasi had demanded reimbursement from South African musician Lebo M after the composer quickly dropped his lawsuit over the viral comedy bit. Jonasi had argued the case was frivolous from the start and aimed at infringing his First Amendment rights. Lebo M (Lebohang Morake) wrote and performed that element of the song, which translates into English as “All hail the king, we all bow in the presence of the king.” In a February appearance on the podcast One54 Africa, Jonasi (Learnmore Mwanyenyeky) joked that the chant actually translates to English as “Look, there’s a lion. Oh my god.” The clip eventually went viral, earning 116K likes on the podcast’s Instagram and pulling in 337K views of the full episode on YouTube. Apparently Morake wasn’t laughing. In a lawsuit demanding $27 million in damages, he accused Jonasi of defamation and other wrongdoing, calling the bit a “fabricated, trivializing distortion, meant as a sick joke for unlawful self-profit.” Jonasi’s attorneys quickly moved to end the lawsuit, arguing that it “targets core First Amendment protections” by trying to “punish” a comedian simply because he had been offended by a joke: “Because the First Amendment is so important in our society, the court should… not allow plaintiff to twist trademark law to suppress free speech.” Rather than fight those arguments, Morake eventually opted to simply drop the case. But Jonasi’s attorneys refused to let him walk away, demanding that he repay the money the comedian had spent defending the case. One of the key provisions of California’s anti-SLAPP law is that it empowers victorious defendants to win such reimbursement after beating a lawsuit. In granting that request on Friday, Judge Staton awarded Jonasi $39,560, representing more than 50 hours spent by his two attorneys who handled the case. Neither side immediately returned requests for comments on the judge's decision.

content: An appeals court has ruled that Bankroll Freddie’s rap lyrics were relevant evidence at his drug trafficking and gun possession trial. A Friday (Aug. 28) ruling from the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals affirms Bankroll Freddie’s 12-and-a-half-year prison sentence for four criminal counts. The Arkansas rapper (born Freddie Gladney III) was convicted in 2024 based on wiretapped phone calls and evidence from a traffic stop — plus, several clips of his rap repertoire. Related Rap On Trial: The Long Battle to Keep Hip-Hop Lyrics Out of Court Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery This included lyrics from “The Last Real Trap Rapper” off Gladney’s 2021 album Big Bank, a joint Quality Control Music/Motown Records release, in which he rapped “448 that’s a pound, 2,500 come and get it now, 224 that’s a half a bow.” The jury also heard Gladney rap, “I got something hot if he think he a bully, switch on the Glock change this b—h to a fully” on his 2020 Ed Dolo collab “Hot.” Gladney’s attorneys argued that these lyrics were not autobiographical, but rather showed him adopting an “artist persona” to make it in the trap rap scene. But in Friday’s ruling, obtained by Billboard, three appellate judges unanimously ruled that the lyrics were “probative to show Gladney’s knowledge of terminology that was alleged to be associated with the sale of marijuana.” “We recognize that some lyrics, rap included, may be prejudicial — sometimes unfairly so,” wrote Judge Jane Kelly in the decision. “But here, the lyrics introduced into evidence were limited to specific lyrics that included words relevant to the charged offenses. No full songs were introduced, and Gladney points to no irrelevant or inflammatory lyrics that were included in the clips.” A lawyer for Gladney, Bobby R. Digby II, told Billboard on Monday (Aug. 31) that he is already in the process of drafting a petition for further appellate review. He declined to comment further on the decision. The use of rap lyrics as evidence in criminal trials is controversial. Critics say it threatens artistic expression and injects racial bias into legal proceedings, and several states have banned or limited this practice for local prosecutions. But rap lyrics are still fair game in federal prosecutions such as Gladney’s. Right now, fellow rapper Lil Durk is also having his lyrics used against him as evidence in an ongoing federal murder-for-hire trial. Legislators have repeatedly introduced a congressional bill that would ban this — the RAP Act — but it has long been stalled on Capitol Hill.

Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter told Billboard that a Los Angeles judge granted their motion to withdraw from the case on Monday (Aug. 31). They did not give a reason for the change but said the 21-year-old “Romantic Homicide” singer (David Anthony Burke) “qualified for appointed counsel.” Related D4vd Murder Case: A Timeline of the Investigation & Charges Over Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s Death Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery “We continue to support David and his defense against these serious charges,” said Berk, Bednarski and Peter. “We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him.” Berk and Peter are both attorneys at the elite Los Angeles entertainment boutique Berk Brettler, whose previous clients have included Marilyn Manson and Armie Hammer. Bednarski also has her name on a private firm, McLane Bednarski & Litt, with a client list that has included former CNN anchor Don Lemon. D4vd’s new attorney is public defender Walid Kandeel. In a Monday statement shared with Billboard, the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office said they are “committed to providing” D4vd with his constitutional right to a defense. “We recognize the loss of life underlying the allegations and extend our sympathies to those who are grieving,” said the office. “At the same time, David Burke is entitled to a defense that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence.” D4vd is accused of stabbing Rivas to death in April 2025 after the 14-year-old threatened to tell the world they’d been having an illegal sexual relationship. Prosecutors say he then chopped up the girl’s body with a chainsaw. Rivas’ decomposing body parts were discovered in an abandoned Tesla registered to D4vd last September. The singer was arrested and charged with first-degree murder, child sexual abuse and mutilating a body this past April. D4vd has maintained his innocence, and his legal team worked to poke holes in the prosecution’s theory during a five-day preliminary hearing last month. But a judge ruled at the end that the evidence, including graphic photos and text messages between D4vd and Rivas, is sufficient to move the case forward toward trial. According to Rolling Stone, D4vd’s new public defender entered a procedural not-guilty plea on the singer’s behalf during Monday’s hearing. He’s next scheduled to appear in court on Oct. 19. A trial date has not yet been set.

content: Jurors heard closing arguments on Monday (Aug. 31) in the murder trial over the killing of Tupac Shakur, with prosecutors telling them that Duane “Keffe D” Davis admitted to “hunting” the rapper — and that his later disavowals of his story “make no sense.” Wrapping up a two-week trial over the long-unsolved 1996 drive-by shooting that left the rapper dead at 25, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis had sought revenge after Tupac beat up his nephew earlier that night at a Las Vegas casino. Related Tupac Shakur’s Murder Trial Is Finally Here, 30 Years After Infamous Hip-Hop Crime Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery “Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” Palal said in the packed courtroom. “So what did he do? He acquired firearms, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr. Shakur.” The case against Davis centers on his own statements, including media interviews and a tell-all memoir, in which he openly admitted to a role in the crime. Davis has since disavowed those statements, and his attorney has argued at trial that his client’s story was fictional and cannot be corroborated by any hard evidence. But in his closing statement on Monday, Palal said the case was “drenched with circumstantial evidence” beyond Davis’ admissions: “It seems like you’ve been told that there’s nothing that exists outside of Mr. Davis’ statements, and that is simply not true.” On the contrary, Palal told the jury that it would “make no sense” that Davis made his admissions as some kind of elaborate fiction: “If the notion is Mr. Davis is creating this whole story, why would he create a story that makes him legally liable for murder when he could just make himself a witness?” In his own closing argument, defense attorney Michael W. Sanft told jurors that Davis’ story was inconsistent — across his own retellings, with testimony from other eyewitnesses, and with evidence like bullet holes. That’s because his client was “telling you fiction as to how this all goes down,” Sanft said. “Why are we here, 30 years later, if Duane Davis truly confessed?” Sanft asked jurors. “When you sit around and you think about a case like this, over 30 years, you have to ask yourself: What did he really confess to that was true?” Sanft said the memoir had been co-written by another author who had made up details about the killing to increase the book’s commercial appeal. He pointed to a media interview years earlier in which Davis appeared to not know key parts of the book: “Is that the reaction of a man who wrote his own book and knows the details of the book?” Monday’s hearing marks the end of a blockbuster trial into Shakur’s killing, which remained unsolved for nearly three decades. Once arguments end, the jury will begin deliberating on a verdict. If convicted, Davis, 63, could be sentenced to life in prison without parole. Shakur, then a rising superstar in the rap world, was killed in September 1996 amid the infamous East Coast-West Coast hip-hop feud, and his death was followed months later by the fatal shooting of rival The Notorious B.I.G. No one was charged with either killing, and the pair of cold cases became a fixture in American cultural history. But in September 2023, prosecutors unveiled a murder indictment against Davis, a former Crips gang leader in 1990s Los Angeles, claiming he’d orchestrated the killing as revenge after Shakur’s entourage beat up his nephew, Orlando Anderson, earlier that night. They cited his own words as evidence, including a 2019 memoir in which he candidly admitted to being in the car and handing the gun to an unnamed shooter in the backseat. At opening statements, prosecutors told jurors that Davis was a key leader of a Compton gang affiliated with the Crips, who had killed Shakur as “an act of revenge” after the fight. They admitted that he “did not pull the trigger,” but said he was a “shot caller” who had “made sure that the shooters were armed and ready to execute their revenge.” Davis’ lawyer Sanft argued back that his client likes to “bullshit” and had repeatedly told a fictional account of the famous killing that could not be backed up by real evidence: “What you’re going to find is that the state cannot prove to you beyond a reasonable doubt the claim that Keffe had anything to do with a first-degree murder.” Across two weeks of trial, prosecutors called 24 witnesses and played more than eight hours of recordings, mostly of Davis himself discussing his role in the killing. Sanft presented only a brief defense case, calling just three police investigators to testify about the killing and its aftermath. At Monday’s closing arguments, Sanft repeatedly stressed a lack of hard evidence to corroborate Davis’ statements. He said prosecutors had shown no proof that his client was even in Las Vegas on the night of the shooting, such as surveillance footage or phone records. He also said some investigation records were missing, and suggested that some police involved with the investigation had been “dirty cops.” “You have no evidence that Davis ever ordered a hit on anyone,” Sanft told the jury at one point. But Palal said the jury had all the evidence they needed to convict Davis of first-degree murder, mostly in the form of his own “textbook admissions” to the famous killing. “For nearly 18 years, Duane Davis has told the police, television, books, YouTube interviewers, anybody that will listen, he has told that he is responsible for the murder of Tupac Shakur,” Palal said in his final remarks. “Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty.”

content: Any industry veteran can tell you… Streaming moves fast. A few years ago, a strong playlist push and a solid release week could carry a lot of the campaign. Now, a song might blow up because of a short-form clip, an older track might suddenly outperform the new single, or a release might get flagged because of fake activity, unclear AI use, or messy metadata. For labels, keeping up with these shifts is part of the job. If you want your artists to thrive, you need to understand how people are finding music, what platforms are worth prioritizing, which numbers actually mean something, and what can put a release at risk before or after it goes live. The best labels aren’t just reacting to whatever happens after release day. They’re watching how streaming is changing as a whole and using that information to make smarter decisions around rollout plans, catalog strategy, promo, monetization, and long-term artist growth. Key Takeaways Total streams are not enough. Track revenue, saves, repeat listening, followers, territories, and catalog activity together. Discovery happens across more surfaces. Short-form video, search, algorithmic recommendations, autoplay, playlists, and catalog tracks can all drive meaningful growth. Release quality and compliance matter more. Accurate metadata, legitimate promotion, clear rights, and responsible AI use can help reduce avoidable platform issues. Catalog is an active growth channel. Older songs can regain momentum years later, so labels should monitor and respond to unexpected activity. Here’s What Labels Need to Know About Streaming Right Now… Paid Subscriptions Are Still Driving Streaming Revenue Streaming is still the engine behind the recorded music business, and paid subscriptions still carry a major part of that revenue. That alone is worth paying attention to, but the real takeaway for labels is that not all streams are worth the same. Fewer streams can still earn more when they’re coming from paid subscribers in places where streaming subscriptions bring in more revenue. The same goes for listener behavior. A fan who saves the track, follows the artist, and comes back next week is more valuable than someone who heard the song once in the background and never engaged again. So instead of only looking at total stream count, it makes more sense to pay attention to things like: Which DSPs are driving the most revenue Where the streams are coming from How many listeners are saving the track How many people are coming back after release week If the release is helping grow the artist’s followers or catalog activity That information should shape what you do next. If one platform is clearly performing better than the others, you may want to spend more time building the artist’s presence there. If one market is reacting more than expected, you could test more content or light ad spend in that area. If people are saving the track and coming back to it, that may be a sign to keep pushing the release instead of moving on right away. Streams tell you how much activity a release is getting, but they don’t tell the full story on their own. In 2026, you should be looking at revenue, saves, repeat listening, and follower growth together to understand if that activity is actually building value for the artist. TikTok, Reels, and Shorts Are Still Pushing People to Streaming Platforms Short-form video is still one of the biggest ways people find music, but attention on TikTok, Reels, or Shorts doesn’t just automatically turn into long-term listeners. The reality is, a song can be used in thousands of videos and still not lead to meaningful streams, saves, follows, or catalog activity. That means the path from socials to streaming needs to be as easy as possible. Don’t wait until tracks start blowing up. From the very beginning, make sure these things are in order: Is the song easy to find by title, lyric, or artist name? Are the artist profiles updated across DSPs? Are the lyrics correct and delivered where possible? Does the link in bio send people to the right track? Is the YouTube page clean and easy to navigate? Are there short-form clips using more than just the chorus? Short-form content can get people interested, but the release setup plays a huge part in what happens next. If the full song is easy to find and the artist profile gives listeners somewhere to go, that attention has a better chance of turning into streams, saves, follows, and catalog discovery. Saves, Follows, and Repeat Listens Are Better Signs Than One Big Spike For a long time, big streaming jumps were treated like the main sign that a release was working. If the song landed on a strong playlist, had a huge first week, or got a sudden bump from socials, that was enough to get everyone’s attention. Now, you have to look closer. A spike can tell you that people heard the song, but it doesn’t tell you if they actually cared about it. The better question is what happened after that first listen. Did they save it? Did they follow the artist? Did they come back a few days later? Did they check out another song? As a label, it’s your job to understand the industry enough to know the best next move. If listeners are saving the track, keep giving them reasons to come back to it. If they’re following the artist, make sure the profile, visuals, and next pieces of content are ready for them. If they’re moving into the catalog, bring older songs into the campaign instead of only pushing the new release. If the spike happens but none of that follow-through is there, you may need to rethink the angle before putting more money behind it. Platforms Are Filtering Low-Quality and Suspicious Activity Harder Than Ever There is more music, more AI-generated content, more fake activity, and more attempts to game the system than ever before. And that has created real problems for DSPs, artists, and listeners. Fake streams can take money from legitimate artists. Misleading metadata can confuse fans. Unclear AI use creates too many issues to count, flooding platforms with low-effort uploads and making real discovery harder for everyone. Now, things are changing. DSPs are cracking down on these issues, and that means as a label, you have to be more intentional and attentive when releasing music. Don’t wait for a platform to catch an issue after the song is already live. Before delivery, make sure you’re checking things like: Is the metadata accurate? Are the artist names, features, credits, and song titles correct? Does the artist profile match the correct artist? Are you avoiding misleading titles, fake features, keyword stuffing, or confusing artist names? Are your promo partners using real, legitimate marketing methods? Is there any sudden activity that doesn’t match the artist’s actual audience? If AI was used, do you know how it was used and where it needs to be disclosed? These checks protect more than one release. They protect your artists, your catalog, your royalties, and your relationship with DSPs. The cleaner the release is from the beginning, the less likely you are to deal with avoidable takedowns, blocked monetization, or platform issues after the campaign is already underway. —— Sharpen your skills… 7 Metrics Every Label Owner Should Check Weekly (And Where To Find Them) Label Branding 101: How to Build an Identity Artists Actually Want to Be Part Of How Music Discovery Algorithms Are Evolving in 2026 Managing Mental Health on Tour: Practical Tips for Artists on the Road —— Older Songs Can Come Back at Any Time Catalog used to be treated like something that lived mostly in the background after the main release cycle was over. Of course, older songs could still earn, but most of the attention usually went to whatever was new. Now more than ever, a song from two, five, or even ten years ago can suddenly start moving because of a short-form trend, a sync placement, a tour moment, a meme, a fan edit, or one lyric people start using online. Think about Imogen Heap’s track, “Headlock.” The song was originally released in 2005, but it found a new wave of attention nearly two decades later after fans started using it in TikTok edits connected to the video game Mouthwashing. Seems random, sure, but that resurgence helped bring the track to a new generation of listeners and even pushed it onto the Billboard Hot 100 for the first time in 2025. When something like this happens, don’t treat it like random activity and move on. Look at where the attention is coming from and what listeners are doing next. Are people saving the older track? Are they streaming other songs from that era? Are they finding it from TikTok, Reels, Shorts, Shazam, or YouTube? Is the activity happening in one specific market? Is the new single pulling people into the catalog, or is the catalog song outperforming the new single? This is where catalog becomes part of the active strategy again. If an older song starts gaining traction, update the visuals, make new content around it, pitch it again where relevant, and give listeners more context around the track. Tell the story behind it. Connect it to the current release. Use it to bring people deeper into the artist’s world instead of letting the moment pass on its own. Playlisting Isn't Just Editorial Anymore For years, getting added to the right DSP playlist could change an artist's entire release, so a lot of teams built their strategy around that one goal. Editorial playlists still matter, but they’re not the only way people find music anymore. A lot of streaming activity now comes from algorithmic playlists, user-generated playlists, radio, autoplay, search, saved libraries, and people coming in from TikTok, Reels, Shorts, YouTube, Shazam, or direct links. All that means is the release needs to be strong outside of the editorial pitch, too. The song title needs to be searchable. The artist profile needs to be clean. The content around the release needs to give people a reason to save it, share it, and come back. The artist’s audience needs to be activated in a way that helps the track keep growing after release week. AI Music Is Changing How Platforms Handle Releases AI music isn’t just a creative conversation anymore. It’s changing how platforms review, label, recommend, monetize, and even restrict releases. For labels, the important thing is knowing how AI was used before anything gets delivered. There’s a big difference between an artist using AI to help brainstorm a melody, using AI-generated cover art, generating a synthetic vocal, or uploading a fully AI-generated track. Those details can affect what needs to be disclosed, where the release can go, and how certain DSPs or monetization tools may treat it. Before submitting anything AI-related for distribution, make sure (at the very least) you know: What AI tool was used What part of the release AI helped create If the tool allows commercial use or distribution If the artist uploaded any third-party vocals, stems, lyrics, artwork, or songs into the tool If the final release imitates a real artist, voice, brand, or existing work If the artist profile represents a real person/group or an AI-made identity A release may seem fine creatively, but if the rights are unclear, the metadata is misleading, or the artist identity creates confusion, it can cause problems after delivery. For a deeper look at how AI-assisted and AI-generated music may affect disclosure, rights, DSP delivery, and monetization, check out our full breakdown: What Creators Should Know About Distributing AI Music in 2026. Final Thoughts… Streaming is always going to change. Platforms will update their rules, listeners will find music in new places, and the numbers you watch today may not mean the same thing a year from now. That’s just the reality of working in this industry. But for labels, that change isn’t something to be afraid of. It’s something to pay attention to. The more you understand how streaming is evolving, the better you can support your artists with decisions that actually match the moment. You can spot real opportunities sooner, protect releases before issues come up, and build campaigns that help songs keep growing after the first wave of attention passes. Streaming will always keep shifting, but with the right strategy, that can be a good thing. For independent labels willing to remain open to change, that just means even more room to grow. Frequently Asked Questions: How can labels tell whether streaming growth is actually sustainable? A strong spike in streams is only one signal. Labels should also look at saves, repeat listening, follower growth, catalog activity, revenue by platform, and whether listeners continue engaging after the initial campaign push. Sustainable growth usually shows up as continued behavior over time rather than one isolated burst of activity. Which streaming metrics should labels prioritize when deciding where to invest more budget? Labels should compare stream volume with revenue, saves, repeat listeners, follower growth, territory performance, and the source of discovery. A market or platform with fewer total streams may still deserve more investment if listeners are saving tracks, returning consistently, exploring the catalog, or generating stronger revenue per listener. How should labels respond when a song gets a sudden spike from TikTok, Reels, or Shorts? First, confirm where the attention is coming from and whether it is translating into meaningful streaming behavior. Then make sure the track is easy to find, artist profiles are updated, links are directing fans correctly, and supporting content is ready. If listeners are saving the song, following the artist, or moving into the catalog, the label can extend the campaign instead of treating the spike as a short-term moment. What should a label do if an older catalog track starts outperforming a new release? Treat the catalog track as an active campaign opportunity. Identify the source of the renewed interest, monitor which audiences and markets are responding, create new content around the song, refresh relevant visuals, revisit pitching opportunities, and connect the renewed attention to the artist's current work. The goal is to turn unexpected discovery into deeper catalog and artist engagement. How can labels identify possible artificial streaming before it creates a problem? Watch for sudden activity that does not match the artist's normal audience, unusual geographic concentrations, unexplained playlist traffic, or large spikes with little corresponding growth in saves, followers, or repeat listening. Labels should also vet promotional partners carefully and avoid any service that guarantees streams, playlist placement, or specific performance numbers. Are editorial playlists still worth prioritizing in a streaming strategy? Yes, but they should not be the entire strategy. Streaming discovery can also come from algorithmic playlists, user-generated playlists, radio, autoplay, search, saved libraries, YouTube, Shazam, short-form video, and direct links. Labels are better positioned when the release can keep growing even if an editorial placement does not happen. How is AI changing what labels need to check before distributing music? Labels increasingly need to understand exactly how AI was used in a release, including whether it contributed to vocals, composition, artwork, lyrics, or the artist identity itself. They should confirm commercial-use rights, review any third-party material uploaded into AI tools, check for imitation or rights conflicts, and make sure the release meets the disclosure and delivery requirements of the relevant platforms and distributor. How often should labels reassess their streaming strategy? Streaming strategy should be reviewed continuously rather than only at the end of a campaign. Labels should evaluate performance during release week, again after the initial promotional window, and whenever there is a meaningful change in listener behavior, platform activity, catalog performance, or market traction. content: The publishing units of Sony Music and Warner Music Group have filed a new copyright lawsuit against Anthropic, claiming the artificial intelligence giant “illegally harvested” more than 20,000 of their songs to train its models. The case, which follows a similar lawsuit by Universal Music Group, BMG and Round Hill, claims Anthropic stole thousands of songs to “fuel Claude,” including “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Mariah Carey's “All I Want for Christmas is You,” and Taylor Swift’s “Paper Rings.” Related Licenses Versus Lawsuits: Why Suno’s Parallel Legal Strategies May Pose a 'Conundrum' Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery “[Publishers] bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history,” lawyers Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music write in a Friday (Aug. 28) complaint obtained by Billboard. The new action comes after similar music lawsuits against Anthropic, an AI behemoth targeting a $2 trillion valuation — first by Universal Music Group and Concord, then more recently by BMG and by Round Hill Music. Major music firms have also brought such litigation against Suno, the leading music-specific AI firm. In the new case, attorneys for Sony and Warner’s publishing units say they “recognize the potential of ethical AI technology,” but that “even the most revolutionary of technologies must develop within the bounds of the law, and Anthropic’s Claude models are no different.” "These acts… inflict immense harm on music publishers and the songwriters they proudly represent," the music companies write. The lawsuit also names Anthropic founder and CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann as defendants. In a statement to Billboard, a spokesperson for Anthropic said: “This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts. Training generative AI models is a transformative fair use — as the court held in [a previous case] — and we will defend ourselves robustly.” AI firms feed millions of works into models to “train” them to create new ones. Dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country over that process, claiming it infringes copyrights en masse. AI companies say training is instead a legal form of copyright “fair use” that fuels innovation. That crucial argument is largely undecided, with billions in damages and licenses hanging in the balance. Like other recent AI cases, Friday’s lawsuit claims Anthropic not only infringed copyrights by using the songs, but also in how it acquired them in the first place. That’s become a crucial element of such cases after a judge ruled last year that even if AI training is legal, using pirated materials to do it is not. “In blatant violation of copyright law, defendants have unlawfully acquired troves of music publishers’ musical compositions,” Sony and Warner write, citing a “brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale.” In that earlier case, Anthropic ended up paying a whopping $1.5 billion settlement after the judge's piracy ruling. Sony and Warner cited that case as evidence of Anthropic’s wrongdoing — and said more legal action was clearly still needed. “Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” the music companies write. “And $1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering $2-trillion-dollar valuation.”

content: Do you remember the great Banana Man controversy of summer 2026? At the Baltimore hardcore band End It’s Toronto show in early June, frontman Akil Godsey called out a guy in the pit for “[wanting] attention” with his banana costume. "You don't get rewarded for doing that shit," he told the crowd. "He wanted the attention, and now he has it." Godsey offered the setlist to whoever stripped off the costume. “People have been trying to dim my sparkle my entire life,” a distraught Banana Man wrote on Instagram after. “I was an unwilling participant, attacked and clothing removed at the direction of a band I paid to see.” Tons of online commenters, many of whom had never heard of End It or been to a hardcore show, had strong opinions about the incident. Godsey became the target of racism and death threats before addressing the situation on his own Instagram. “We’re a hardcore band,” he explained. “We do hardcore things.” Finally, three weeks after the incident, End It called a truce with banana-costumed concertgoers when Godsey hugged it out with a different Banana Man at Jera On Air. He was also handed a banana that he promptly tossed into the crowd. “Who woulda thought doing something stupid at a show would get me a month of attention?” Godsey said. Now the great End It Vs. Banana Man Feud Of 2026 has our attention again. Yesterday Godsey showed off new No Banana Man ink he got at Baltimore’s Red Thorn Tattoo, posting the reveal on his Instagram Stories. content: The iconic Reason Rack has been a core component of the Reason DAW since its launch in 2000. But in 2019, it was made available as a standalone plugin for the first time, offering producers the chance to harness its power within DAWs outside of Reason. Reason Rack is highly acclaimed, and allows producers to stack virtual instruments on top of one another with total control over the routing between them. Now, Reason Studios has unveiled a new free version, offering 15 Reason instruments, effects and creative utilities for no cost at all. This isn’t a trial, and has no expiration or watermark, Reason confirms. READ MORE: Polyend has unveiled a new MIDI controller – and it looks an awful lot like a QWERTY keyboard Reason Free – what’s actually included? Credit: Reason Studios The 15 included Devices consist of four virtual instruments, five effects, and six creative utilities. The flagship virtual instrument available within Reason Free is Europa, a powerful wavetable synthesizer geared towards “modern sound design”, with three spectral engineers, advanced waveform shaping, modulation and effects, and a bank of over 600 presets for instant inspiration. The full list of included Devices is below: Instruments Europa – Powerful wavetable synthesizer for modern sound design Kong – Versatile drum machine for beats, samples and percussion ID8 – All-in-one collection of essential songwriting instruments Monotone – Monophonic synthesizer for deep basses and expressive lead Effects Scream 4 – Creative distortion and saturation The Echo – Flexible stereo delay with modulation and filtering Audiomatic – One-knob effect for vintage and lo-fi character RV7000 MkII – Professional reverb for realistic and creative spaces MClass Maximizer – Mastering limiter for louder, cleaner mixes Creative utilities Scales & Chords – Creates melodies and chords that stay in key Combinator – Combines instruments and effects into custom devices Pulsar – Dual modulation device for adding movement to any Rack parameter Spider Audio Merger & Splitter – Splits and combines audio signals Spider CV Merger & Splitter – Routes and combines modulation signals MIDI Out Device – Controls external plugins and hardware How is Reason Free different from the full Reason Rack? Where Reason Free offers 15 instruments, effects and utilities, the full Reason Rack – included in a Reason+ subscription – offers more than 90, as well as weekly Sound Packs, plus access to the full Reason DAW. Also included in Reason+ is access to the LANDR ecosystem, with unlimited music distribution and tools for creativity, mixing and mastering. Additionally, Reason users can expand their setup with individual Rack Extensions and Refills, or by buying a perpetual Reason licence. What is Reason Studios saying about Reason Free? Credit: Reason Studios “Reason has always been about musical exploration – when you connect two Devices, turn the knobs, and discover a great sound you weren’t looking for,” says Mattias Häggström Gerdt, Product Manager at Reason Studios. “With Reason Free, we’re giving everyone a piece of that experience. The included Devices are fantastic in their own right, but the Rack also gives you the freedom to go deeper, experiment and build something entirely your own.” Pricing & availability As the name might suggest, Reason Free is totally free, and is available now as a VST3, AU and AAX plugin for compatible DAWS. “It is free forever, with no trial period, expiration date or watermark,” Reason Studios says. Additionally, Reason Free can run as a DAW of its own, offering producers up to 16 tracks. Learn more at Reason Studios. content: Instagram’s new First Draft feature automatically trims clips and removes pauses to create a starting point for Reels. Here’s what it means for creators and artists. Instagram has introduced First Draft, a new feature that automatically edits video clips into a starting point for a Reel. The idea is simple: help creators spend less time editing and more time creating. For creators and independent artists already juggling music creation, promotion and social media, it could make turning existing footage into social content a little quicker. What is Instagram First Draft? First Draft automatically creates an initial edit from the clips you select for a Reel. It trims down clips, removes pauses and silences, and brings the footage together into a rough cut. Instagram says the process can create a first draft in seconds, meaning creators can skip some of the more repetitive parts of editing and get to refining their video sooner. The feature is currently rolling out on iPhone. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Instagram’s @Creators (@creators) How does Instagram First Draft work? There are two ways to use Instagram’s First Draft feature. From the Reels gallery, select one or more clips and tap the First Draft button. Instagram will then create an initial edit that you can review before moving into the full editor. You can also access First Draft directly after filming through the Instagram camera. Importantly, First Draft isn't intended to make all of the creative decisions for you. Instagram describes it as a starting point rather than a finished video. That distinction is reflected in the name, too. It's a First Draft, not a final cut. Everything it does is reversible, meaning you can reorder, remove and adjust clips before moving into Instagram's full editor. How could First Draft be useful for artists and creators For independent artists, First Draft could make it easier to turn existing footage into regular Reels. Whether it's clips from a gig, studio session, rehearsal or day in the life of an artist, there's often plenty of potential content sitting on a phone. The time-consuming part is turning those clips into something worth posting. First Draft can handle some of the initial trimming, giving artists a starting point to work from rather than editing every clip from scratch. The feature isn't particularly revolutionary, with similar automated editing tools already available in apps such as CapCut and Adobe's editing software. However, bringing the functionality directly into Instagram means creators can do more without leaving the platform. It also fits into Instagram's wider push to make content creation easier. The platform has introduced several creator-focused tools this year, while Meta continues to develop its dedicated Edits video editing app. Instagram updates its Edits app with new creator tools For artists trying to maintain a consistent presence on social media alongside making and releasing music, anything that reduces the time spent on repetitive editing could be useful. content: A US judge has allowed UMG and Sony to pursue Suno over alleged YouTube ‘stream ripping’ to train its AI models. Here's what artists need to know. A US judge has allowed Universal Music Group and Sony Music to add a new claim against AI music company Suno, alleging it bypassed YouTube's technology to download copyrighted recordings for AI training. Here's what the case could mean for musicians, producers and the future of AI-generated music. The legal battle between the music industry and AI music generators has taken another significant turn. A US federal judge has given Universal Music Group (UMG) and Sony Music Entertainment permission to pursue a claim accusing Suno of using so-called “stream ripping” to obtain copyrighted recordings from YouTube and use them to train its AI music models. The decision doesn't mean Suno has been found guilty of piracy. Instead, Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV has ruled that the labels have presented a plausible enough case for the claim to move forward while the court examines the evidence. For musicians and producers, however, the development is significant. The case highlights one of the biggest questions surrounding generative AI in music: where does the training data come from, and should artists be paid or asked for permission when their recordings are used? What is ‘stream ripping’? The term might sound technical, but the basic idea is fairly straightforward. The labels allege that Suno obtained music from YouTube by using software designed to download audio from online videos. Their amended complaint names open-source tools including YT-DL and YT-DLP, alleging that Suno used them to bypass YouTube's technical protections and extract copyrighted recordings. At the centre of the new claim is YouTube's “rolling cipher”, a technical measure that the labels say is designed to prevent unauthorised access to underlying media files. The labels argue that bypassing this technology amounts to circumvention under Section 1201(a)(1) of the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA). Suno has previously disputed the legal basis of this argument, including questioning whether the technology in question actually controls access to the copyrighted works in the way required by the DMCA. Judge Saylor said determining exactly how the technology and downloading tools work will require more evidence. For now, though, he found that the labels' allegations were sufficient to proceed. This is separate from the bigger copyright question It's worth making a distinction here. UMG and Sony are already suing Suno over the alleged use of copyrighted sound recordings to train its AI system. The stream-ripping claim is an additional legal argument focused specifically on how the recordings were allegedly obtained. The court has not yet decided whether Suno's use of copyrighted recordings to train its AI model constitutes fair use. That question remains one of the central issues in the case, with fact discovery scheduled to close on September 30, 2026, according to the latest reporting. The parties are then expected to seek summary judgment on the wider question of whether training an AI model on copyrighted recordings without a licence can qualify as fair use. In other words, there's still a lot to be decided. Why this matters to independent artists For independent musicians, this isn't simply another major-label legal dispute. The argument over AI training affects anyone whose music is publicly available online. Independent artists often upload their music to YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud and other platforms specifically because they want people to hear it. But being publicly available doesn't necessarily mean an artist has agreed for their recordings to be downloaded, copied and incorporated into an AI training dataset. That's one of the biggest tensions in the current AI debate. Listening to a song and using a song to build a commercial AI model are two very different things. The music industry is increasingly asking where that line should be drawn. Independent artists are already taking Suno to court The major labels aren't the only rights holders pursuing Suno. Country artist Tony Justice, alongside his label and publishing company, has brought a proposed class action against Suno representing independent artists, songwriters and producers. In August, Judge Saylor refused to dismiss most of that case, allowing claims involving alleged AI output infringement and the alleged circumvention of YouTube's technology to proceed. The case is particularly relevant to independent musicians because the plaintiffs argue that creators outside the major-label system also need meaningful protection as AI companies build increasingly powerful music-generation tools. That could make the coming months particularly important for independent artists. The music industry is moving towards licensing Interestingly, while Suno continues to face litigation, the company is also beginning to move towards licensed music. In August, Suno announced a deal with BMG covering recorded music and publishing repertoire, with the agreement described as opt-in for artists and songwriters and intended to settle Suno's previous use of BMG's catalogue. Suno has also said that it plans to introduce a new generation of models “developed in partnership with the music industry”, while retiring its previous models. That shift could prove important. Rather than the industry having to decide whether AI music should exist at all, the bigger question may increasingly become what a fair AI music ecosystem looks like. That could include licensing agreements, artist opt-in systems, compensation models and clearer rules around training data. AI isn't going away, but the rules are changing The Suno case comes at a time when governments, streaming services, record companies and artists are all trying to establish where AI fits into the music industry. Recent developments have included streaming platforms introducing greater transparency around AI-generated music, while Australia's ARIA Charts has moved to exclude fully AI-generated recordings from chart eligibility. Meanwhile, a German court recently ruled that Suno infringed copyright by processing songs without the necessary rights in a case brought by German collecting society GEMA. Suno has said it is considering its options, including an appeal. The direction of travel is becoming increasingly clear: AI companies are going to face more questions about where their training material comes from. What should artists be doing? For independent artists, there's no need to panic or stop using AI tools altogether. Instead, be more careful about understanding the tools you're using. Before incorporating AI-generated material into a commercial release, check the platform's terms around ownership, commercial use, training data and licensing. Keep track of how your music is created, particularly if you're using AI alongside your own recordings or production. It's also worth keeping your original project files, stems and recordings. As AI identification and rights-management systems become more sophisticated, having a clear record of your creative process could become increasingly useful. And, as always, make sure your music is properly registered and distributed with accurate metadata. The bigger picture for musicians Perhaps the most important takeaway from the Suno case is that the AI music debate is moving beyond “Can AI make music?” It clearly can. The harder questions are now about ownership, consent, compensation and transparency. If an AI company can legally license music from artists and rights holders to train its models, there is a potential path towards an ecosystem where technology and human creativity can coexist. But if copyrighted music can simply be scraped from the internet and used without permission, independent artists could find themselves competing with systems trained on the very music they spent years creating. That's why this case matters even if you've never used Suno. The decisions being made now could influence how music is created, distributed and monetised for years to come. For independent artists, the best response is to stay informed, understand where AI fits into your own workflow and keep building your catalogue and audience. The technology is changing quickly, and the rules around it are changing just as fast. Distribute your music for FREE with RouteNote! content: Released a new song and the streams aren't coming in? Don't panic. Here's how independent artists can turn a disappointing release into useful momentum for the next one. Releasing new music is exciting, but it can also be a little brutal. You spend weeks or months writing, recording, mixing and preparing a track, only to see surprisingly few streams once it finally goes live. Before you decide the song has failed, take a breath. Low streams don't necessarily mean you've made a bad song. For independent artists, getting music heard is often a gradual process, and one release rarely tells the full story. Give your release time It's easy to obsess over the numbers during the first few days, but don't treat release day as a final verdict. Unless you already have a large audience waiting for your music, it can take time for a track to reach new listeners. Instead of asking why your song hasn't gone viral, think about whether you've given people enough opportunities to discover it. One Instagram post announcing your release probably isn't enough. Keep the song active across your social channels and look for different ways to introduce it. Share the story behind the track, post a performance, show how you produced a particular section or highlight a lyric you love. You don't need to repeat the same promotional message over and over; find different stories within the same release. Look beyond the stream count Streams are an obvious metric, but they're not the only indication that your music is connecting with people. Look at saves, follows, playlist additions, comments and repeat listeners. A smaller number of genuinely engaged listeners can be far more valuable than thousands of passive plays. Your analytics can also help you understand where people are discovering your music. If listeners are coming from your artist profile, playlists, social media or algorithmic recommendations, each tells you something different about your audience and promotional strategy. Use that information rather than simply refreshing your stream count. Don't forget about the song itself Sometimes your promotion needs improving. Sometimes the song simply hasn't found the right audience yet. Think about who your track is actually for. Are you putting it in front of people who already listen to your genre? Are you working with other artists or creators who have a similar audience? Are you submitting to relevant playlists rather than simply chasing the biggest numbers? The goal isn't to get your song in front of everyone. It's to get it in front of the right listeners. And don't be tempted by services promising thousands of guaranteed streams. Artificial streams don't create fans and can put your release at risk with streaming platforms. Building an audience might take longer, but genuine listeners are what you actually want. Keep the song alive Your release doesn't have to disappear after the first week. If you still believe in the track, keep finding new ways to present it. Perform it live, create an acoustic version, share a behind-the-scenes clip or revisit it when you have a new idea for content. A song can find its audience weeks or even months after release. Music doesn't suddenly become irrelevant because it didn't perform immediately. For independent artists, this is particularly important. Without a major label campaign constantly pushing your music, you have to give your strongest songs room to breathe. Use the experience to improve your next release Every release is an experiment. Maybe your best-performing content was a simple studio clip rather than an expensive music video. Perhaps listeners responded strongly to one particular part of the song. You might discover that one platform consistently sends more engaged listeners than another. Take note. Your next release can benefit from everything you've learned from the previous one. This is also where having a reliable distribution strategy matters. Making sure your music is correctly delivered across the major streaming and social platforms gives potential listeners more opportunities to discover you. RouteNote helps independent artists and labels distribute their music while retaining control over their releases. One quiet release doesn't define your career It's easy to attach your emotions to a number. But a song getting 200 streams instead of 2,000 doesn't mean you've failed. Building a music career is usually about consistency, experimentation and gradually finding your audience. Some releases will perform better than others. Some songs will surprise you. Others might only find their audience much later. So don't delete the song, don't buy streams and don't give up. Work out what you can improve, keep promoting the music you believe in and take those lessons into your next release. Distribute your next release for FREE with RoueNote! content: SoundCloud has spent years being the place where you stumble across your next favourite artist. Now, it wants to be the place where you actually buy their music, too. The company is currently testing a new feature that lets artists sell and deliver music directly from their SoundCloud profiles, meaning fans can discover a track, decide they want to own it and buy the download without being sent off to another platform. Artists can set their own prices and offer music in formats including MP3 and WAV. More importantly, SoundCloud takes no commission from those sales. Once standard fees and taxes are deducted, artists keep 100% of the revenue. READ MORE: How to get playlisted on streaming services: 7 playlist pitching tips It’s a notable addition to a platform that has traditionally been much better at getting music heard than getting it sold. A stream might introduce an artist to a new fan, but a direct purchase puts actual money into the artist’s pocket. SoundCloud says there’s already a sizeable appetite for that. Around 250,000 artists currently direct fans to external platforms to buy their music, with 2.4 million tracks linked to purchase pages. The company says more than 500,000 SoundCloud users are sent to those external sites every year, while 28% of surveyed artists either already sell downloadable music or want to start. The feature will initially be tested with 200 US-based Artist Pro creators. Feedback from the beta will help shape the service before it rolls out to all eligible creators later this autumn. Participating artists will be able to monitor their sales through Artist Studio and the Fan Support Dashboard. Direct sales will also add to SoundCloud’s existing artist monetisation tools, including Fan-Powered Royalties, Fan Support, on-demand vinyl and ticketing. “Artists should be able to build their audience in one place, on one platform,” says SoundCloud CEO Eliah Seton. “SoundCloud has always been where artists find their first fans and build real communities. We’re continuing to bring more of what they need to grow their careers into that same experience, while letting fans directly support the music they love.” SoundCloud’s move follows the lead of Bandcamp, which has long championed direct-to-fan music sales and launched its Bandcamp Fridays initiative in 2020. From streaming trends and playlist activity to territory growth, UGC performance, royalties, and more, that level of information can become overwhelming to the untrained eye. Especially when you're managing multiple artists and releases at a time, you need to know which numbers are actually worth paying attention to. Some metrics show momentum. The best labels in the game understand not only what to look at, but what that information is telling them and how to use it to make better decisions across their roster. In this post, we’re breaking down 7 metrics every label owner should check weekly, where to find them, and how to use them to keep everyone moving in the right direction… Key Takeaways Weekly change matters more than the biggest number. A smaller track accelerating quickly may deserve more attention than a larger release that is holding steady or declining. Never evaluate a spike by itself. Compare streams with playlist activity, territory growth, UGC, saves, audience behavior, and platform performance to understand what is actually driving momentum. Look for signals that repeat across platforms. When the same city, audience, song section, or behavior appears across streaming, social, video, merch, or ticketing data, you have stronger evidence of a real opportunity. Turn every meaningful metric into a next action. Growth in a territory might justify localized promotion, while strong YouTube activity, playlist traction, or UGC may call for completely different support. Operational data deserves the same attention as marketing data. Reviewing splits, payees, recoupments, royalties, and payouts every week can prevent small backend issues from becoming larger artist relationship problems. What Your Weekly Label Data Is Really Telling You Weekly Stream Movement Streams are usually the first place labels look, but the real value isn’t only in the total number. What you really want to pay attention to every week is how your active releases, artists, and catalog are moving overall. Is an active release gaining week over week? Did one artist’s catalog spike suddenly? Did the whole release drop after promo ended? Are streams shifting between partners, playlists, or territories? This gives you the weekly pulse of your label before you zoom in on individual tracks. For example, one release with 75,000 streams this week may look like the obvious priority at first glance… But if it had 150,000 streams last week, you need to figure out what changed before you put more energy behind it. Did it lose a playlist placement? Did release-week promo end? Did paid spend stop? Did one territory drop off? If the stream drop came from one playlist, you may need to shift focus toward content, user playlists, or another round of pitching. If the drop happened across every platform and territory, the release may need a completely new creative angle before more budget makes sense. On the other hand, a song that jumped from 4,000 streams to 12,000 streams in a week may be showing early traction. That’s when you dig into where the growth came from. For example, if most of the increase came from Mexico City, you can test localized ads, pitch regional playlists, or have the artist post content that speaks directly to that audience. If the growth came from YouTube, check if fans are using the song in videos or if a creator posted something that drove people back to the track. If you’re a Symphonic client, you can check this in your SymphonicMS account under Analytics, then Streams. From there, you can view daily stream data across your catalog and break it down by partner, artist, track, release, playlist, and territory. The whole point of checking this metric is to spot the biggest shifts across the label first, then decide where you need to look closer. Top Tracks by Growth After you check overall stream movement, look at which individual tracks increased the most from the previous week. Not just the tracks with the highest total streams, but the ones that saw the biggest jump compared to where they were before. This can help you catch momentum early, especially across a larger roster. A smaller track going from 1,000 to 5,000 streams in a week may need more attention than a bigger track holding steady at 80,000. When you see that kind of jump, look into where it came from. If it came from a playlist, check how long the placement has been active and if the track is still growing outside of that playlist. If it came from one city or country, consider localized content, ads, or pitching. If it came from YouTube, TikTok, or UGC, find the post, creator, or usage pattern that started the increase and build around it. You can find this in the same place as your weekly stream movement in SymphonicMS under Analytics > Streams. From there, review track-level performance and use the partner, territory, playlist, artist, and release filters to understand where the growth is coming from. Playlist Activity Playlist activity is one of the easiest metrics to misread. A playlist add can give a song a real boost, but it can also make a release look bigger than it actually is if most of the streams are coming from one place. Instead of only looking at the stream spike, look at what happened around it: Did the song keep growing after the playlist add? Did listeners save it or add it to their own playlists? Did the placement lead to more streams across the artist’s catalog? Did the track start moving in new territories? Did the lift continue after the playlist placement ended? In the same place you checked stream movement and track growth in SymphonicMS, you can also see playlist details like track position, playlist streams, and how the placement is changing over time. So if a playlist is driving streams for a few days and everything drops right back down after, that placement may have helped with exposure, but just not deeper fan movement… That’s not necessarily a “bad” thing. It just means the track might need stronger artist-led content, a better follow-up post, another pitching angle, or more support around the part of the song people are reacting to. If the playlist activity leads to saves, followers, user playlist adds, catalog listening, or growth on other platforms, that’s a stronger sign the placement is actually helping the song reach people who will stick around. —— Want to learn more? Check these out: Onboarding Artists: What Indie Labels Should Have in Place Before Signing Anyone Content Strategy for Labels: How to Stay Consistent Without Burning Out Smart Budgeting Basics for Indie Labels That Actually Work Sync Licensing for Indie Labels: How to Prep Your Catalog the Right Way —— Territory Growth A release may be performing steadily overall, but when you look closer, you might see one country or city growing faster than the rest. When this happens, look closer. This could be a sign that a new audience is forming naturally in that market, and a little extra support there could make all the difference. Genres like Latin, Afrobeats, Caribbean, dancehall, electronic, hip-hop, metal, and other communities don’t move the same way in every market. A track may hit first in the artist’s home country, but it can also start growing somewhere completely different because of a playlist, creator trend, local scene, DJ support, diaspora audience, or fan community that picks it up early. When you’re in your SymphonicMS account, take a moment to check the territory breakdowns. Next, compare what you’re seeing there with Spotify for Artists, YouTube Studio, TikTok for Artists, Meta, Bandsintown, Shopify, or even your ticketing data. If the same cities keep showing up across streams, social engagement, video views, merch orders, and show interest, that market deserves a closer look. From there, now you have a real market to build around. Test a small ad budget, pitch regional playlists, reach out to local creators, or shape content around the audience that’s already responding. Want to learn more about building from international traction? Check out How To Monetize Your Music in New Global Markets as an Independent Artist to learn how to turn this early traction into real growth. Partner and Platform Performance When you’re managing multiple releases, artists, and campaigns at once, you can’t go full throttle on every platform for every song. A track may be doing most of its streaming on Spotify, but getting stronger engagement on YouTube. Another may be steady overall, but quietly overperforming on Apple Music, Audiomack, Beatport, Pandora, or another platform that better matches the genre. Checking partner performance helps you see where the release is getting the clearest response; then you can shape the next moves around that. In SymphonicMS, look at your partner breakdowns alongside your track, playlist, and territory data. Look for: Which platform is driving the most activity Which DSP is growing faster than the others Which genre-specific platforms are showing early movement Which platforms are performing better in certain territories Which platform response lines up with the support you’re already giving the release From there, the next move should be a lot clearer. A song gaining on YouTube may need more video support. A track picking up on Beatport may need DJ-focused promo. A release overperforming on one DSP in a specific territory may need more local pitching instead of another broad campaign. Let the data guide you. Social and UGC Activity Social and UGC activity shows how people are using the music, not just listening to it. That could mean a Reel with the hook, a fan edit on YouTube, a TikTok using the beat drop, or an older track getting picked up because one lyric fits a moment. Pay attention to what repeats. If multiple creators keep using the same lyric, intro, beat drop, or emotional part of the song, that gives you something to build around. Don’t force the campaign around the chorus if people are naturally reacting to the first 10 seconds. Also look at who is responding. Age, gender, location, and audience behavior across socials and DSPs can help you understand who the campaign is actually reaching and how to target the next move. A track may be getting strong UGC from younger listeners on TikTok, but stronger streaming activity from 25-34 year-olds on Spotify or YouTube. That can shape your ad targeting, content style, playlist strategy, and which markets you prioritize next. You can also check YouTube UGC and Meta Analytics in your SymphonicMS account to see how your catalog is being used across user-generated content. From there, compare it with TikTok for Artists, YouTube Studio, Instagram Insights, Spotify for Artists, or Shazam. Look at available audience data too, like age ranges, top cities, saves, profile visits, watch behavior, and repeat engagement. If UGC is growing but the streams are flat, the content may not be pushing people to the song yet. If UGC, streams, saves, Shazams, profile visits, and audience trends are all moving together, that’s a stronger sign the content is helping people find the music and take another step with it. Royalty, Split, and Payout Health This is the less glamorous side of running a label, but it’s one of the most important metrics to check every week. Strong streaming numbers don’t mean much if splits are wrong, payees are missing information, recoupments aren’t updated, or royalty details haven’t been reviewed. In SymphonicMS, check your Royalty Summary, SplitShare, and payout details to make sure everything is tracking correctly. Look for anything that could slow down or complicate payments. Things like: Missing payee information Incorrect splits Recoupments that need review Unusual adjustments Releases that aren’t earning the way you expected This is also where you can compare activity to revenue. A track may have fewer streams but stronger earnings because of where those streams came from. Another release may be getting a lot of activity but not generating the kind of revenue you expected, which means it’s worth looking closer at partner, territory, or rights details. For labels, especially, this is also about trust. Artists and collaborators want to know they’re being paid correctly and on time. Checking this weekly helps you catch small issues before they turn into bigger conversations later. Some Final Thoughts… Checking your metrics weekly doesn’t mean obsessing over every small change. It means staying close enough to your catalog to understand what needs your attention before the moment passes. When you know what’s moving, where it’s moving, and what might be causing it, you can make better calls across your roster. You know when to keep pushing a release, when to adjust the strategy, when to support a new market, when to clean up a payout issue, and when to let the data lead you somewhere different altogether. Great label management comes down to paying attention and staying informed about the industry. The numbers won’t make the decisions for you, but they can absolutely show you where to look next. Good luck! Frequently Asked Questions Which music metrics should an independent label check every week? Independent labels should monitor weekly stream movement, top tracks by growth, playlist activity, territory growth, partner and platform performance, social and UGC activity, and royalty, split, and payout health. The most useful insights come from comparing these metrics together rather than judging any one number on its own. How can a label tell whether a streaming spike is real momentum? A streaming spike is more meaningful when other signals rise with it. Look for increases in saves, user playlist adds, UGC, catalog streams, followers, Shazams, or activity in new territories. If streams jump because of one playlist and fall immediately when the placement ends, that may be temporary exposure rather than lasting audience growth. How should labels decide which tracks deserve more marketing support? Look at the rate of growth, not just total streams. A track climbing from 1,000 to 5,000 weekly streams may represent a stronger emerging opportunity than a larger track holding steady at 80,000. Then identify what caused the increase, such as a playlist, territory, creator, platform, or piece of content, before deciding where to put more budget or promotion. When should a label invest more heavily in a new territory? A single week of stronger streams is worth investigating, but repeated signals make the opportunity much stronger. If the same city or country keeps appearing across streaming growth, social engagement, video views, Shazams, merch sales, ticketing interest, or fan activity, it may be time to test localized ads, regional playlist pitching, creator outreach, or market-specific content. What should a label do when UGC is growing, but streams are not? First, identify what people are actually reacting to, such as a lyric, beat drop, intro, or creator trend. Then look at whether the content gives viewers a clear path back to the song or artist. Growing UGC with flat streams can mean the content is resonating socially without yet converting into deeper listening behavior. How often should an independent label review royalties and payout information? A weekly operational check can help catch missing payee information, incorrect splits, outdated recoupments, unusual adjustments, or unexpected revenue patterns before they become bigger issues. Labels should also compare revenue with streaming activity because the releases generating the most streams are not always the ones generating the strongest earnings. How long should a label wait before changing strategy based on weekly data? Not every week-over-week movement calls for an immediate strategy change. First determine whether the shift is isolated or showing up across multiple signals. A sudden playlist loss may explain a short-term decline, while several weeks of falling streams, weaker engagement, and declining platform activity may point to a broader slowdown that deserves a new approach. The software synthesiser experts focused on weight, impact, and motion with this new design. A press release from the team ahead of the Pure SUB release reads: “In modern electronic music, from dubstep and drum & bass to the wider world of club and bass-driven production, low-end has become the defining voice. READ MORE: Dreamtonics’ Instrument X can create a digital orchestra that sounds like real musicians “Over the past decade, bass has moved from the foundation under the track toward the front of it. It’s not unusual now for a producer to spend hours on a single sub - sculpting harmonics, distortion and movement until the bass is the hook, the signature, the drop. “With the rise of sound design as a craft, a sound once felt and forgotten is now designed with the care once reserved for the lead. Pure SUB is a synthesiser built for that one job.” Included in Pure SUB is a three-way split between sub, harmonics, and texture which can “morph timbre through a dual-mode engine built for everything from clean 808s to wide Reese, then blend in noise and texture so the bass cuts through on any system”. The new kit will also reshape harmonics through more than 40 filter modes. Arturia adds that this will “drive the timbre with the Sub Processor - a bass-focused chain of expert-built modes that distort, texturise and transform in a few moves”. New motion tools are also featured as part of the Pure SUB kit which offers three envelopes, six customisable modulators and full keyboard expressivity. This includes MPE, layer samples and noise, animation for any parameter, and modulation even to the modulators themselves. Pure SUB will also have new tools for distorting in the FX rack, a preset randomiser to offer up new ideas with its “instant new sound” option, and a resampling tool that can give every note or bounce a “slightly different” sound.
