These changeable keys are also backlit. The company also says it's looking into making the firmware behind Keys open source. “Alternative layouts, different control modes, custom MIDI tools, sequencers, and other ideas can all be explored through software,” it says. Keys isn't tied to the computer, either, with a TRS MIDI output enabling direct connection with external synths, drum machines, or other MIDI hardware. It can also be used as a standalone controller. “Nine rotary controls can be freely assigned to MIDI CCs for controlling software or hardware, or mapped to everyday computer functions like volume, scrolling, and brightness. A built-in display gives you feedback as you make adjustments,” the brand continues. Polyend says Keys is still in its prototype phase, so “functionality, colour, or hardware could change”. content: Luminate is introducing a new framework designed to identify and measure AI-generated music, with ‘AI Generated’ labels coming to its CONNECT platform later this year. For independent artists, labels and distributors, the move could signal a new era of transparency around how AI is used in music. AI-generated music is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Streaming platforms are receiving enormous volumes of AI-created tracks, while artists, labels and rights holders are trying to understand how this rapidly expanding catalogue is affecting discovery, royalties, charts and the wider music ecosystem. Now, one of the music industry's most important data companies is taking a major step towards making that activity easier to track. Luminate has launched a new framework for identifying and measuring AI-generated music, with its CONNECT platform now capable of flagging AI-generated songs and artists worldwide. The new labels are expected to become visible to CONNECT customers and partners later in 2026. For independent musicians and labels, this is another important development in an industry where transparency around AI is quickly becoming part of the normal release process. What is Luminate's new AI music framework? Luminate is best known for its music consumption data, with its information helping power Billboard's charts and providing industry professionals with insight into streaming, sales and audience behaviour. Its CONNECT platform brings together data on artists, songs and releases, allowing music companies to analyse performance, consumption and market trends. The new AI framework adds another layer to that system. Luminate says CONNECT can now identify AI-generated songs and artists, with the company having already identified thousands of AI-generated items in its database. The classifications aren't visible to users yet, but Luminate says the labels will roll out to customers and partners later this year. Songs and recordings identified as fully AI-created will receive an “AI Generated” label. There will also be separate classifications for artists. An “AI” label will indicate an artist confirmed to be fully AI-generated, while “Human” will only be applied to artists individually confirmed by Luminate's screening process. Importantly, Luminate says that a lack of an AI or Human label doesn't necessarily mean something has been confirmed as human-made. The company hasn't yet processed its entire database through the identification system. How will Luminate identify AI-generated music? Rather than relying on one detection method, Luminate is building its framework around three different sources of information. The first is Luminate's own identification technology. Its data science team analyses artists and songs in CONNECT, looking at streaming data and metadata before using audio identification technology to help confirm potential AI-generated material. The second element is data supplied by streaming platforms. As DSPs develop their own systems for identifying AI-generated music, Luminate says it will be able to incorporate that information through its existing partnerships. The third is attribution information from AI music companies themselves. Luminate says it is in discussions with AI music companies about receiving information directly from the source, potentially allowing AI-generated content to be identified before it reaches a streaming service. That combination could eventually give the industry a much clearer picture of how AI-generated music moves from creation to distribution to consumption. Why does this matter now? The timing is significant. AI-generated music has grown at a remarkable pace, creating a challenge for platforms and rights holders trying to distinguish between human-made, AI-assisted and fully AI-generated music. Luminate CEO Rob Jonas said the growth of AI music has moved faster than the industry's ability to consistently identify and measure it, arguing that greater visibility is needed to understand trends, assess fraud risks and make informed decisions. The scale of the issue has become increasingly obvious. In July, Deezer said it was receiving close to 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks per day in June, accounting for more than half of new tracks delivered to the service on peak days. That's a huge amount of music entering the ecosystem. And while AI music itself isn't necessarily a problem, the sheer volume creates questions about discovery, streaming manipulation and how royalties are distributed. For independent artists, that's where the issue becomes particularly relevant. AI music isn't automatically the problem It's important to separate AI-assisted music creation from music that is generated almost entirely by AI. Many human artists already use AI tools in some part of their creative process. They might use AI for brainstorming, sound design, mastering, editing, production assistance or other elements of their workflow. That doesn't necessarily mean the finished recording is an entirely AI-generated work. Luminate's current framework is specifically focused on identifying recordings that are fully AI-created, while its artist classifications are intended to identify artists that are fully AI-generated. That's an important distinction for musicians. The conversation around AI is moving beyond the simple question of whether an artist has used AI at all. Increasingly, the industry will need to understand how AI was used, how much of a recording was generated by it and where human creativity remains central. That could become increasingly important for artists as platforms develop their own AI policies. Spotify, Apple Music and other platforms are also moving towards AI labels Luminate's announcement is part of a much wider industry trend. Streaming platforms have started developing their own approaches to AI transparency, with Deezer already identifying and tagging AI-generated music. Apple Music announced in August that it will label songs that are materially generated using AI, while Spotify has announced an “AI Persona” badge for artist profiles built around AI-generated identities. Spotify also says music from those AI Personas will be kept out of editorial and algorithmic recommendations by default. That means AI disclosure is increasingly moving from being something discussed by industry organisations into something listeners may actually see. For artists, that's worth paying attention to. The metadata attached to your music is becoming more important, and transparency around how a track was created could increasingly influence how it is treated by platforms and industry databases. Could AI labels affect the charts? This is where Luminate's announcement becomes particularly interesting. Luminate provides the data behind Billboard's charts, meaning the company's ability to identify AI-generated music could eventually have implications for how AI tracks are measured within the wider music industry. However, Luminate has not said that its AI labels automatically determine chart eligibility. That's an important distinction. Billboard has separately committed to identifying AI use on its charts and in its editorial coverage, while industry bodies are developing their own policies around whether fully AI-generated music should be eligible for certain charts. The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) and a group of major and independent music companies recently proposed principles that would keep fully AI-generated recordings off official charts unless certain conditions around authorisation, human contribution and fraud are met. Australia's ARIA Charts has also moved to exclude wholly AI-generated tracks from its charts and awards under its updated rules. So while Luminate's system isn't itself a chart-eligibility policy, it could provide an important piece of the infrastructure needed to enforce future rules. What does this mean for independent artists? For independent musicians, the most important takeaway isn't necessarily that AI-generated music is about to be banned or pushed out of streaming. It's that transparency is becoming increasingly important. If you're using AI tools as part of your creative process, make sure you understand the terms attached to those tools. Check what commercial rights you receive, whether the service allows distribution and whether you need to disclose AI involvement. It's also worth keeping records of your creative process. That might include project files, stems, songwriting notes, original recordings and information about which tools were used during production. You may never need to provide that information. But if a track is incorrectly flagged as AI-generated, having evidence of your creative process could become useful. Luminate says flagged content will have a dedicated review process, allowing artists and labels to respond if they believe an AI classification is incorrect. That's particularly important as automated identification systems become more widespread. AI detection won't be perfect No identification system is likely to get everything right. Luminate itself acknowledges that its database hasn't been fully processed and that some AI-generated content may not yet receive a label. The company says it is continuing to expand its coverage. For artists, that means an AI label shouldn't necessarily be treated as an absolute statement about how a track was created. There will inevitably be false positives, missed detections and grey areas. That's why Luminate's review process is potentially important. As these systems become more influential, artists need a way to challenge incorrect classifications rather than simply accepting an automated decision. The bigger issue, music discovery is getting noisier Perhaps the biggest reason this matters for independent artists is the effect AI could have on music discovery. Streaming platforms already contain enormous catalogues. Every day, thousands of new tracks compete for attention. Now add tens of thousands of AI-generated tracks to that ecosystem. The challenge isn't simply that AI music exists. It's that a huge increase in supply can make it harder for listeners to find the music created by artists they genuinely want to follow. That's why we're likely to see more sophisticated filtering, recommendation systems and transparency tools. For independent artists, this makes artist identity more valuable. A listener who discovers you isn't just choosing one song. They're potentially choosing an artist to follow, a catalogue to explore and a story to become invested in. That human connection is something a label on a database can't create for you. What artists should do now There's no need to panic about Luminate's announcement. Instead, use it as a reminder to get your digital music strategy in order. If you're releasing music independently, make sure your metadata is accurate and that your artist name, credits, ISRCs and release information are consistent across platforms. If you use AI during production, understand exactly what your chosen tools allow you to do commercially. Don't assume that being able to generate or download a track automatically means you have unrestricted rights to distribute it. And if you're creating predominantly human-made music, keep evidence of your creative process where practical. Most importantly, keep building your artist identity. Your music, social presence, live performances, collaborations and relationship with your audience all help distinguish your project from the enormous volume of content now entering streaming services. Distribution is only part of that process, but it's an important one. RouteNote gives independent artists and labels a way to distribute their music across major streaming and social platforms while maintaining control over their releases. As AI changes the volume and visibility of music online, having a clear release strategy, and making sure your catalogue is properly managed, will only become more important. A new standard for AI music transparency? Luminate describes its new framework as a starting point, rather than a finished solution. That's probably the most sensible way to look at it. The music industry is still figuring out how AI should be identified, labelled, measured and regulated. Streaming platforms are developing their own systems, AI companies are negotiating licensing arrangements and chart organisations are introducing new eligibility requirements. There isn't one universal standard yet. But Luminate's involvement is significant because CONNECT sits so close to the data infrastructure used by the wider music industry. If Luminate can combine its own identification technology with data from DSPs and AI music companies, it could eventually give labels, publishers, managers and artists a much clearer understanding of where AI-generated music is appearing and how it is performing. content: BBC Introducing is expanding its support for emerging artists with a month-long series of live events across the UK this November, following the removal of its long-running stage from Reading & Leeds Festival. BBC Introducing is giving emerging artists a new reason to get their live sets ready, announcing a major programme of events taking place across the UK throughout November 2026. The month-long Introducing LIVE programme will visit 10 locations, bringing together live performances, workshops, open mic sessions, educational panels and networking opportunities for up-and-coming musicians, DJs and music creators. The announcement comes shortly after the BBC Introducing Stage was removed from this year's Reading & Leeds Festival after 18 years. For independent artists, the new programme could provide an important alternative route to live exposure at a time when opportunities for emerging musicians are increasingly valuable. BBC Introducing takes its live support on the road Introducing LIVE will take place across Belfast, Bridgend, Gateshead, Glasgow, Leeds, Liverpool, London, Manchester, Nottingham and Sunderland throughout November. The programme begins on November 5 with events in Bridgend and London before continuing around the UK. The month will finish with four special showcases in Leeds on November 28. Alongside performances, the programme will feature industry-focused activities designed to help artists develop their careers, including workshops, panels, open mics and networking opportunities. There will also be a songwriting camp in Manchester and a takeover event at The Fire Station in Sunderland, which will feature panels, workshops, open mic sessions and an industry feedback centre. BBC Introducing editor Kelly Betts said that championing and nurturing artists and creatives remains at the heart of the platform, describing this year's Introducing LIVE as its biggest edition yet. For artists still finding their feet in the industry, that combination of performance and education could be just as useful as the chance to get on stage. The announcement follows the removal of BBC Introducing from Reading & Leeds The new programme arrives at an interesting moment for BBC Introducing. In July, it was confirmed that the BBC Introducing Stage would no longer appear at Reading & Leeds Festival, ending an 18-year run at the event. Since launching in 2008, the stage had become one of the festival circuit's best-known platforms for emerging talent. Artists including Ed Sheeran and The 1975 played the stage early in their careers, while the BBC said around 70% of British artists on the 2026 Reading & Leeds lineup had previously been supported by BBC Introducing. The removal wasn't presented as an end to emerging-artist support at the festival. Festival Republic said its new Canopy stage would provide a platform for a wider pool of up-and-coming artists, with organisers arguing that opening the stage beyond BBC-selected acts could create opportunities for a more diverse range of new musicians. BBC Introducing also confirmed that it would continue working with other festivals, including The Great Escape and Latitude, to support emerging artists. Why live opportunities matter for independent artists For an independent musician, getting discovered online is only part of the equation. Streaming platforms can help listeners find new music, while social media allows artists to build audiences directly. But live performance offers something different: a direct connection between artist and audience. A strong festival performance can introduce an artist to hundreds of people in a single afternoon. It can also create opportunities to meet promoters, other musicians, managers, photographers and industry professionals. That's particularly important for artists who are still building their careers. A festival slot isn't necessarily going to result in an overnight breakthrough. But it can provide footage for social media, photographs for an EPK, new followers, future bookings and a chance to demonstrate that an artist can perform confidently in front of a crowd. The BBC Introducing model has historically been built around this combination of discovery and development, rather than simply putting new artists on a stage and sending them on their way. It's more than just a gig One of the most useful aspects of Introducing LIVE for emerging artists is the wider programme surrounding the performances. Workshops and educational panels can give musicians access to information that isn't always easy to find when you're working independently. Networking events can also provide an opportunity to meet people who could become collaborators or industry contacts further down the line. For newer artists, simply being in a room with other musicians and people working in the industry can be valuable. The live music industry can sometimes feel difficult to break into from the outside. Events that bring artists and industry professionals together can help make those connections more accessible. A reminder to independent artists, keep building your live profile The BBC Introducing announcement also highlights the importance of being ready when opportunities appear. If you're hoping to play festivals, showcases or support slots, having a professional live setup and a clear artist profile can make a difference. That means having your strongest songs ready, an up-to-date EPK, good-quality live footage and a clear online presence. It also means making sure your recorded music is easy to find when someone discovers you after a show. For independent artists using digital distribution, keeping your catalogue organised across major streaming platforms is another important part of that process. A new listener who discovers you at a live event should be able to search your name and immediately find your latest music. Platforms such as RouteNote allow independent artists and labels to distribute their music across major streaming and social platforms, helping turn those real-world discoveries into longer-term listeners. BBC Introducing remains an important route for new music Despite the change at Reading & Leeds, the latest announcement suggests BBC Introducing isn't stepping back from emerging artists. If anything, it is taking a broader approach. Rather than concentrating its live activity around one major festival stage, Introducing LIVE will bring opportunities to artists in cities across the UK. That geographical spread could be particularly valuable for musicians outside London's traditional industry hubs. And that matters. The UK has a huge community of independent artists creating music outside the biggest cities and established industry networks. Bringing workshops, performances and networking events to places such as Sunderland, Gateshead, Bridgend and Belfast creates more opportunities for artists to participate without necessarily having to travel to London. For musicians trying to build a career from the ground up, accessibility can make a real difference. What should artists do next? If you're an emerging artist, it's worth keeping an eye on BBC Introducing's upcoming opportunities and making sure your artist profile is ready for them. But don't wait for one particular festival or showcase to validate your project. Keep releasing music. Keep performing wherever you can. Build relationships with local venues and other artists. Capture your live performances and use that material to strengthen your online presence. And when an opportunity like Introducing LIVE comes along, you'll be in a much stronger position to take advantage of it. The removal of BBC Introducing from Reading & Leeds might have closed one door for emerging artists, but this new programme suggests the organisation is keen to open several more. For independent musicians, that's a development worth paying attention to. Distribute your music for FREE with RouteNote! Simply put your chosen sounds in the associated clips, follow the instructions, such as when to cut the low frequencies, and the final product will be a complete song because the arrangement is based on a track that’s worked on dancefloors around the world. Each stencil also clearly labels drops, breakdowns, and other sections to help users get a feel for what each part looks like in a session. “Producers download Serum packs to practice sound design and MIDI packs to practice music theory. We were blown away that nothing like that existed for arrangement. The advice is always to pick apart your reference tracks, but there's nothing visual to check your work," says Kevin Rea, co-founder of Colour With Live. “Our mission isn’t for our stencil to be a crutch that you rely on for every song, but instead something that you can learn from and then apply to future productions.” Rea and his fellow co-founder, Grant Hunter, came up with the idea for Stencils because, like many young producers, they have to work full-time on top of working on their music. After coming home from a long day, they wouldn’t know where to start when they were staring at an empty Ableton window. Stencils allowed them to get their creativity flowing and finish songs. Now, they have created over 250 Stencils in a variety of genres such as UK Garage, Dubstep, Tech House, Drum & Bass, Techno, and Hip-Hop. For a limited time, they are offering a free pack of three Stencils based on Flip It by Levity, Fisher’s rework of World Hold On by Bob Sinclar, and Dimension’s Once In A Lifetime. The update adds a new timbral extraction engine, where users can drop in any sound and Abyss will reconstruct it as a ‘palette’ of tone colours, automatically tuned and ready to play. Other highlights in Abyss 2 include a polyrhythmic sequencer, a new effects chain with four slots and 20 effects to populate them, various workflow improvements, and over 200 new presets. Abyss 2 is available from Dawesome for intro pricing of £69 (full price £119), or existing owners can upgrade for £35 (full price £60). Cherry Audio – Memorymode 2 It seems to be the week for sequels, with Cherry Audio releasing a major update to Memorymode, significantly expanding the capabilities of its Memorymoog-inspired polysynth plugin. According to the developer, its analogue modelling has been significantly improved using cutting-edge analysis and emulation techniques, delivering more accurate oscillators, filters, and envelopes. The effects section has been upgraded with three independent effects chains and 22 studio-quality effects, including the new Wide Phaser and Rotary Speaker. The Version 2 update also adds support for polyphonic aftertouch and MPE, letting users create more expressive patches, and the preset browser has been redesigned as well. Memorymode 2 is available from Cherry Audio for $69, with upgrade pricing available to existing owners when they log into their accounts. JMG Sound – Continuum JMG Sound has launched Continuum, a delay plugin inspired by the gritty imperfection of classic hardware units. It features two identical but independent delay engines, letting users mix and match from three models — Tape, BBD, and Digital — with a Mojo parameter for exaggerating the unique physical characteristics of each one. The signals of each can then be mixed using the Crossfeed controls, with a Diffuse control that uses all-pass filters to smear the edges into blooming, reverb-like spaces that can be further tailored with modulation and damping. Users can also set their delay repeats to follow organic, humanlike grooves and syncopation. Need somewhere to start? Use the intelligent randomisation button. Continuum is available from United Plugins for intro pricing of £13 (full price £68). Sonible – Smart:chain Sonible has launched Smart:chain, described by the developer as ‘the intelligent channel strip’. It combines EQ, compression, de-harshing, gating, input riding, saturation, and leveling, all within one intelligent, AI-assisted plugin. According to Sonible, Smart:chain’s processors can analyse your audio and interact to create a coherent processing chain, rather than operating independently. As each plugin instance can communicate with the others across your session, it’s easy to manage tracks within the context of the entire mix using smart depth staging, and you can even access every Smart:chain instance in a single window. Smart:chain is available from Sonible for intro pricing of £85 (full price £149), and there’s a 40% education discount available for students and teachers too. Codwaves – BassXtend Closing this week’s round-up is another mix tool, this time from Codwaves. Named BassXtend, the plugin is designed to make 808s, synth and bass guitar, and kicks more perceptible on phones, earbuds, and laptops. How does it do it? It generates harmonics based on the pitch of the incoming signal, and the ear reconstructs the fundamental frequency, even though it can’t be reproduced on smaller speaker drivers. BassXtend offers four simple controls: Intensity, Root (which acts as the crossover point), gain trim, and Low Band In/Out. Crucially, it only generates harmonics above the crossover point you set, so it won’t add headroom-eating low frequency content. Booking-Agent.io is a real-time booking search engine, not a venue directory: you type in an artist you sound like and it returns the venues, promoters, and talent buyers tied to that artist's actual show history, with verified contacts unlocked by credits. Because it searches live data, the contacts reflect who is booking right now, not who booked two years ago. How do you book gigs as an independent artist without a booking agent? Start from proof, not cold pitches. List 10 to 20 artists at your level, find the rooms that already book them, then reach the talent buyer or promoter for each room by name rather than emailing a general venue inbox. A real-time tool like Booking-Agent.io does that research in minutes by pulling venues and verified talent buyer contacts from a similar artist's live history. Is Booking-Agent.io a good Sonicbids alternative for booking your own shows? They solve different halves of the problem, so the honest answer is that it depends on what you need. Sonicbids is best known as an electronic press kit tool, great for packaging your bio, music, and photos into one link. Booking-Agent.io starts a step earlier, at the question of who to send that press kit to: type in an artist you sound like, and it returns the venues, promoters, and verified talent buyers tied to that artist's real performance history. Many artists use an EPK tool to build the pitch and Booking-Agent.io to find the right person to send it to. What is the best alternative to a venue directory like Pollstar or Gigwell for independent artists? Industry directories are excellent if you are an agency that needs a broad standing reference and has the budget for it. For an independent artist booking their own run, the gap is that a directory tells you a venue exists, not who is booking it right now or which rooms actually fit your draw. Booking-Agent.io works the other way around: it is a real-time search engine, so you start from an artist you sound like, and it surfaces the specific venues, promoters, and talent buyers from that artist's live history, each with a verified contact. You are reading who is booking today, at your level, instead of scrolling a list built for a different tier of act. What does a booking agent cost once you have one? It varies, but most work on commission, commonly 10 percent and sometimes up to 15 percent. It's real, ongoing work, which is exactly why they wait for artists who can already fill a room. How far ahead should you book? It depends on the room and the market, but reaching out well before your target date and keeping your dates geographically close gives you the best shot at a clean, profitable run. content: EQ, or equalization, is a tool that allows us to control and modify the tonal makeup of audio. This is useful to correct imperfections and to enhance certain tonal characteristics while reducing others. How does EQ work? EQ tools work by boosting or cutting the amplitude (i.e, volume) of specific frequencies within a sound. EQ processors typically include multiple ‘bands’. Each band operates around a specific frequency, and different types of band will affect the surrounding frequencies in different ways. What are the different types of EQ band? Credit: Minimal Audio Parametric / Peak: Creates a bell- or trough-like curve centred on the band’s frequency. The width of the curve is controlled by the “Q” or “Bandwidth” setting. Low Shelving: Progressively cuts or boosts frequencies that lie below the band’s frequency. Typically, some frequencies that lie above the band’s frequency will also be affected High Shelving: The functional opposite of a low shelving band. Impacts frequencies that lie above the band’s frequency. Low Cut: A low cut band is the same as a high-pass filter, and so blocks frequencies that fall below the band’s frequency. High Cut: A high cut band is the same as a low-pass filter, and so blocks frequencies that lie above the band’s frequency. It is the functional opposite of a low cut filter. What are the different types of EQ processor? EQ plugins and processors usually combine multiple types of bands into a single unit. These are the three most common varieties: Studio- or console-style EQ: Typically combines a low-shelving and high-shelving band with two parametric bands. Sometimes also includes low- and high-cut bands. Pultec-style EQ: Based on vintage outboard EQ processors. Typically handles cutting and boosting as separate bands. Band frequency selection is usually stepped rather than continuous. Graphic EQ: Combines a number of fixed-frequency, fixed-width peak bands. Band boost/cut is controlled by a fader. The pattern of faders creates a graphical curve, hence “graphic” EQ. When should I use EQ? EQ is used extensively at all stages in the recording process. Input conditioning: Hardware EQs and preamps/recording channels that include EQ are useful for optimising the recorded sound, countering mic colouration, and correcting obvious problems. Tracking: Use temporary EQ during tracking to create a comfortable working mix. Also use on cue mixes to enhance/reduce prominence of elements the performer needs to hear more/less clearly. Mixing: Use to sculpt and shape the frequencies of your parts to give each its own spectral space within the mix, and to help bring the parts together into a cohesive whole. Mastering: Use tightly-focused / high-Q EQ to fix specific frequency issues; use broad low-Q EQ to make gentle changes to the overall tonal balance. Which EQs should you use? All DAWs come with at least one type of EQ plugin, and often include multiple varieties. You're certainly able to garner pro-grade results with the EQs in your DAW, or any free EQs that are out there. However, if you're looking for an EQ with expanded features, a different interface, or would like an emulation of a classic hardware EQ, you might want to look around the third-party plugin marketplace. content: 60 years ago, Jimi Hendrix first plugged in and played through a Marshall amplifier – and it was the start of a true musical love affair. Instantly, Marshall amps became a key component in Hendrix’s legendary guitar tones. To honour its Hendrix’s relationship with Marshall amps, the brand is releasing the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Collection. Over the year, Marshall has released a slew of guitar gear, including the 1959 JMH Half Stack inspired by Hendrix’s own rig and limited-edition Fuzz Face pedal. But Marshall has left the best ‘til last; the Anniversary collection is gaining three new additions, in the form of sleek new headphones, a speaker, and a new hand-made amplifier inspired by the iconic Studio Vintage amp. READ MORE: “For him, reverb was green, distortion was red”: Eddie Kramer on Jimi Hendrix seeing effects in music as colours First up, the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition Major V headphones will allow fans to listen to Hendrix classics on the go. With a foldable design, the headphones are perfect to pop in your bag but still pack a crisp, Marshall-standard listening experience. If you’re keen to share your Hendrix listening experience with others, the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition Emberton III might be up your alley. Complete with the collection’s signature cosmic, purple design, with a silver all-seeing eye on the media jog and purple LEDs. Each silicon sleeve is also unique, due to them all being hand-dipped in a water transfer print. Credit: Marshall Now for the pièce de résistance – the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition JMH Studio Bundle. The hand-made from quality plywood and wrapped in black Tolex, the amp is based on the classic Studio Vintage amp and promises to provide “expressive cleans and deep blues textures”. The 20W valve head comes with power reduction to 5W, two bridgeable channels as well as two ECC83 preamp valves, an ECC83 phase splitter, and two EL34 power valves There’s also a switchable series effects loop. The amp also wears a comic-inspired black and purple psychedelic pattern across its control panel alongside purple LEDs. Silver beading is also across the entire amp, with Hendrix’s beloved all-seeing eye motif also sitting on the top and bottom of the stack. Credit: Marshall “The story of Jimi and Marshall has always been personal to me because I first heard it from my dad, Al Hendrix,” Hendrix’s sister, Janie Hendrix, explains. “Dad was there and shared those memories with me, so I carry that story only one degree from its source.” “Jimi was always searching for a sound that did not yet exist, pushing beyond what anyone thought an electric guitar could do,” she continues. “Marshall gave him the power and freedom to turn those bold ideas into a sound the world had never heard before. Sixty years later, that connection between Jimi and Marshall still speaks to new generations of musicians who are pushing creative boundaries and searching for their own sound.” In terms of other artists searching for their own sound, American blues-rock artist Ally Venable had the honour of trying out the new Marshall Studio Vintage JMH before anyone else. As she experiments with her tone on the new bit of kit, she explains just how Hendrix and Marshall shaped her musical journey. In terms of pricing, the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition Major V headphones will set you back £129.99. As for the speaker, the Emberton III costs £149.99, while the JMH Studio Bundle amp is £1,749.99. In terms of Hendrix, rare new footage of Jimi Hendrix’s legendary 1969 Woodstock show has also recently surfaced online. Captured by a student who snuck onstage, the hour-and-a-half video gives an entirely new perspective on the legendary show. The collection is available to order from 25 August, with retail availability beginning 9 September 2026. For more information, head to Marshall. In the lead-up to a release, a strong promo strategy can help build anticipation and drive early fan engagement. But here’s the problem: without a follow-up release, tour, or campaign, excitement builds and peaks on release day, then quickly fades. It’s a cycle independent artists endure, but it doesn’t build a fanbase. That’s where a waterfall release strategy helps. Instead of releasing a full album all at once, you roll it out gradually through single releases. This keeps fans coming back, helps you reach new listeners, and gives each track from your larger project more room to shine. In this blog, you’ll learn how to set up a waterfall release and use it to boost streams, deepen fan relationships, and get more long-term value from your music. What is a waterfall release strategy? A waterfall release strategy allows you to release an album or EP in increments, releasing individual singles that you can stack to direct traffic back to previous releases. In simple terms, the waterfall approach is: Release a single ahead of the album release Release a second single, including the first single in this release, too Release a third single with the two prior singles, and so on… Why should I use a waterfall release strategy? Waterfall releases help you build anticipation and momentum ahead of a full project, boosting streams by promoting each track individually over time—rather than all at once. This approach has many benefits for independent artists looking to get the most out of their full-length releases. Extend the lifespan of your release: Turn each track into a mini-campaign to keep momentum going. Maximize playlist opportunities: Releasing separate singles allows you to pitch each on to Spotify Editorial playlists and maximize other playlist placements. Work with the algorithm: Steady, spaced out releases drive consistent engagement which platform algorithms reward. Attract new listeners: Singles are easy entry points for new listeners. Each release builds curiosity and draws fans deeper into your music. How do I use a waterfall release strategy? You can use the waterfall approach on your next release by following the steps below. The key to this approach is maintaining accurate ISRCs and metadata to allow streaming data to carry over on re-released tracks. 1. Choose your singles and prepare artwork for each release Identify a few tracks you want to release ahead of your album. Typically, artists release 3 singles that capture different sounds and themes from the longer-form work. The waterfall strategy requires new artwork for each release. Avoid using your intended ultimate album art for your singles as it will be unusable for your album without cancelling the prior release that uses it. 2. Choose a distributor CD Baby makes it easy to waterfall your release and get your music on over 150 streaming platforms worldwide. 3. Decide on a release schedule Once you’ve decided what singles you want to release and how you’ll distribute them, decide the order and timing of each single leading up to your album. It’s typical to give at least a month of space between releases to give each track sufficient time in the spotlight. 4. Submit your first single Submit your track through a distributor like CD Baby and follow your typical release strategy for a single, but boost anticipation by mentioning it’s a track off an upcoming full-length album. 5. Re-release your first single with a second single About a month after your first single, release a second single along with the first single, using the same ISRC for Single 1 to re-release, along with a new UPC and album artwork. If you’re distributing with CD Baby, note that our release creation process defines a single release as one track only, and an album release as two tracks or more. More information here. 6. Re-release your first and second singles with a third single After another month, release your first two singles with a new third single. Again, create new artwork and a UPC for the release, but use the same ISRCs for Singles 1 and 2 to carry over your streams. You can promote each of your singles as a standalone release, following our ultimate music release strategy guide for 2025 for best results. Important Reminder: Match your Metadata and ISRCs In order to carry over your streaming data every time you re-release a track, you must ensure the metadata and ISRC codes match the original track. Details on how to find your ISRCs here. Conclusion Ready to get started? Trusted by a growing community of over two million independent artists, CD Baby is with you every step of the way—from release to promotion—offering easy distribution to over 150 streaming platforms worldwide and marketing tools and insights to grow your fanbase. Get Started FAQs How do I pay for a waterfall release with CD Baby? The waterfall release is a strategy, not a CD Baby product. As such, you’ll need to purchase a separate submission for each release — from your first single to your final album. When the full album is ready to come out, can the track order be different from the waterfall order? Absolutely. Track order will always appear in the order you’ve entered for a release upon submitting it for distribution. How many singles should I waterfall before dropping a full album? You can release as many singles as you like before dropping a full album, but be aware that as track number or total runtime accumulate, digital streaming platforms might start showing releases as albums rather than singles. content: As of August 2026, AI music policies are changing fast. This article reflects the latest guidance available at the time of writing, but creators should always review current platform, distributor, and tool-specific terms before submitting a release. Whether you like it or not, AI is here. In the music industry, artists are using AI tools to make demos, test song ideas, generate vocals, create cover art, build music videos, and in some cases, create full tracks from scratch. But there’s a big difference between using AI as part of your creative process and using AI to copy another artist, impersonate a real person, mislead listeners, or flood DSPs with low-effort uploads. At Symphonic, we believe there is a responsibility to support creators who are experimenting with new tools while still protecting artists, rights holders, platforms, and fans from misuse. We believe the problem starts when AI is used in ways that create confusion around rights, ownership, identity, or intent. If a track was made with AI, that needs to be disclosed. If you upload something, you need to know where it came from, what tool made it, and what that tool actually allows you to do with the final track. If the release imitates someone else, misrepresents what it is, or tries to game the system, that crosses a line… Although the rules around AI music are still changing, a few things are clear. If you’re thinking of submitting any AI-assisted or AI-generated music, here’s how to do it responsibly. AI Music Distribution in 2026: What Artists Need to Know Before Releasing Anything Be Clear About How AI Was Used Before you submit a release, be honest about where AI showed up in the process. Was it part of the audio? The artwork? The video? Did it help shape the writing, production, vocals, or final master? Did it generate the entire track? Someone could’ve used AI to generate a quick melody idea, then rewrote and recorded the full song themselves. Another artist might’ve used AI to create cover art. Someone else might’ve used a platform like Suno to generate most of the audio. Those are all very different situations. How AI was used affects what you might need to disclose, what terms you should review, and how the release may be handled by different platforms or partners. That’s why it’s important to know exactly how AI was used before you submit anything for distribution. The main thing is to be clear about what YOU actually made. If AI helped create part of the final release, be honest about that. Know exactly what tool you used, what it generated, and how that output ended up in the finished product. When distributing through Symphonic, you’ll need to disclose these details so the release can be reviewed and delivered responsibly based on how AI was used and what each DSP currently requires. How To Know If You're Allowed to Distribute What You Made Before you submit AI-related music, separate three questions: How was the track made? Was AI used for a prompt, a demo, a vocal, a stem, a master, the artwork, the video, or the full recording? Do you have the rights needed to distribute it? Did the AI platform give you the right to commercially use the output? Did you upload anything into the tool that you don’t fully own or have permission to use? Will every DSP, monetization tool, or rights management program treat it the same way? Not always. A release may be distributable in one context but still face extra review, disclosure requirements, promotion limits, monetization restrictions, or platform-specific rules somewhere else. Start by checking the terms of the AI platform you used. Look for anything that explains: Commercial use Ownership Monetization Licensing Prohibited uses User-generated content Download rules Plan-specific rights Those sections usually tell you what you can and can’t do with the audio, artwork, lyrics, vocals, or video the tool helped create. Pay attention to the plan you were on when you made it, the date you created or downloaded the content, and the current terms tied to that output. Some platforms treat free users, paid users, and enterprise users differently, and those terms can change over time. A paid subscription also doesn’t automatically mean every release is cleared for every type of distribution, monetization, or platform use. Suno’s recent Terms update is a good example of why this matters. Its new Terms of Service take effect September 3, 2026, and Suno has said the update will clarify rights around user content, commercial use, and downloads. That doesn’t mean every creator’s situation is identical. It means artists need to check the plan they used, when the content was created or downloaded, and what the current terms actually allow before assuming something is safe to release. Look at what you put into the tool. Ask yourself: Did I upload samples, stems, vocals, lyrics, artwork, or another artist’s song as a reference? Did I use anything I don’t fully own or have permission to use? Did my prompt ask for something that sounds like a real artist, brand, or specific copyrighted work? If the input creates a rights problem, the output will probably create one too. Keep a simple record of what you used and when. Save the platform name, the date you created the content, the date you downloaded it, the account or plan you used, and any terms tied to that output. Screenshotting the relevant terms can also help just in case they change later. If you can’t clearly explain where the content came from, what tool helped make it, and what that tool allows you to do with it, don’t submit the release until you can. Do Not Use AI to Copy, Impersonate, or Mislead AI can be part of your creative process, but it shouldn’t be used to fake, copy, or confuse people. That’s where responsible use turns into misuse. Symphonic does not allow content that clearly infringes on existing copyrighted works, intentionally mimics or impersonates real artists, brands, or individuals without authorization, or uses misleading metadata. We also don’t allow spam, mass-generated low-quality uploads, or attempts to manipulate DSPs. In simple terms: don’t use AI to make people think they’re hearing someone they’re not. Don’t title, tag, or package a release in a way that misleads listeners or platforms. Don’t use AI to flood stores with low-effort tracks just to chase streams. If the release depends on confusing people to work, it’s not something you should be submitting. Not Every Platform Treats AI Music the Same Way DSPs, platforms, and monetization programs all have different rules around AI-generated or AI-assisted content. A release can be okay for one DSP and still need extra review, disclosure, or restrictions somewhere else. For example, right now: Audible Magic, Meta, Bandcamp, and YouTube Content ID do not accept works created with generative AI. Apple Music and Vevo require AI disclosure for music videos if AI was used in the creation of the video. Spotify has announced AI Persona badges for artist profiles that represent AI-generated artist identities rather than real people. Starting in mid-September 2026, music from AI Personas generally will not be included in Spotify’s editorial or algorithmic recommendations by default, unless listeners show intentional engagement signals like following the AI Persona artist. Some monetization and rights management tools may have stricter requirements than standard distribution, especially when the release involves fully AI-generated audio, AI-generated vocals, or unclear rights. That Spotify update is important because AI disclosure is no longer just an administrative step. It can affect how a release or artist profile is surfaced, recommended, promoted, and monetized. Using AI as a creative tool is one thing. Building a public artist identity around an AI-generated persona is another, and platforms are starting to treat those situations differently. If those details are missing or wrong, your release can get held up, blocked from certain platforms, or lose access to monetization tools you were counting on. In some cases, it can create problems after delivery too, meaning something you thought was already live and handled may need to be reviewed, corrected, restricted, or taken down. Being upfront doesn’t mean every platform will accept the release, but hiding or leaving out AI details can definitely make things worse. Creators Should Have a Say in How Their Music Is Used by AI At Symphonic, we believe if an AI company wants to train on real music, creators should have a say in how their work is used, what permissions are attached to it, and whether they want to participate at all. That’s why we partnered with Sureel AI. Through this partnership, participating artists can opt in to fully licensed AI datasets instead of having their music used without permission or outside a clear licensing framework. For creators, this means if you want your music included in licensed AI datasets, there can be a path to do that where you can be fairly compensated. If you don’t, your work shouldn’t be treated like it’s automatically up for grabs just because it’s on the internet. “AI represents real opportunity for artists, but only if we use it correctly,” explains Jorge Brea, our Founder and CEO at Symphonic. “By giving our artists the chance to opt in to Sureel’s fully licensed AI datasets, we are pushing back against unpaid training and opening new revenue opportunities for those who wish to participate.” Questions to Ask Before You Submit AI-Related Music Before you submit an AI-assisted or AI-generated release, take a minute to check the basics. Ask yourself: Did AI help create the audio, artwork, video, lyrics, vocals, production, or final master? Did I disclose AI use where required? Do I know which platform or tool was used? Did I check the terms for that tool? Did I upload anything into the tool that I don’t fully own or have permission to use? Does the release imitate a real artist, voice, brand, or existing song? Am I trying to use AI to make something real, or am I flooding platforms with low-effort content? Am I expecting this release to qualify for every DSP, monetization tool, or rights management program? If any of those answers are unclear, don’t submit yet! Figure it out first. It’s better to fix the issue before delivery than to deal with the takedown, rejection, or blocked monetization after the release is already in motion. Protect Your Music Before It Gets Misused AI doesn’t only affect the music you’re making next… It can also affect the music, vocals, and catalog you’ve already released. At a recent conference we attended, there was an artist speaking about how their voice was used without their consent, and their work was used in ways they never agreed to, by people they’ve never even heard of. As a company run by musicians, this is something that we personally feel for. The idea that someone can take your voice, your sound, or your catalog and use it without permission is unsettling, especially when it feels like there’s nothing you can do about it… That’s one of the reasons we’re happy to have recently partnered with ArtyShield, the AI trust infrastructure platform built to help artists, labels, vocalists, and rights holders protect their music and voices from unauthorized AI use. Through this partnership, Symphonic clients can access tools like: MusicShield, which helps protect tracks from being used to train AI models without consent while keeping the audio quality intact. VoiceShield, which helps protect vocal performances from unauthorized cloning, synthesis, and synthetic voice misuse. We aren’t fully anti-AI. We just strongly believe artists should have real tools to protect their work, their voice, and their identity as this technology keeps evolving. Symphonic clients can now access ArtyShield directly through the Client Offerings section in SymphonicMS. Getting started is free, with paid tiers available for clients who need deeper protection and expanded access to ArtyShield’s tools. Ready to try it out? Log in to your SymphonicMS account to check it out today. Final Thoughts… AI is evolving fast, and the truth is, it’s going to bring both positives and negatives to the music industry. For artists, the goal isn’t to fear every new tool or jump into every trend without thinking. The goal is to stay informed and make sure the way you use AI still respects the people and work behind the music. At Symphonic, we believe there’s a future where AI can support creativity without replacing accountability. That future depends on transparency, permission, and giving creators the power to choose when they want to participate… and when they don’t. Now in its 15th edition, BOmm continues to be a key market for artists and music professionals looking to make real connections, share ideas, and expand into new territories. For 2026, BOmm is also opening its call to international artists for the first time, creating even more opportunities for cross-border exchange and collaboration. At this conference, you’ll experience things like: Conference Programming: Talks, workshops, conversations, and sessions with music industry leaders covering the trends, challenges, and opportunities shaping the business today. Showcases: Live performances from selected artists and bands, giving attendees the chance to discover new talent from Colombia and beyond. BOmm Connect: One-on-one business meetings designed to help artists, managers, agencies, labels, and other music professionals create new opportunities, partnerships, and deals. content: “How do I get my music on Spotify playlists?” is one of the most common questions we get from independent artists at CD Baby. It’s no surprise — popular playlists like Spotify’s official editorials can skyrocket an artist’s streams overnight. But bad actors have also recognized the power these playlists have — and built an entire industry around faking them. These actors create playlists that use bot activity to drive up their streams. This artificial streaming activity can ruin artists’ algorithmic standing and at worst, get their music removed from the platform. In this blog, we’ll run through five ways to avoid Spotify playlists that employ artificial streaming and conclude with a bit of perspective on how playlists should fit within your strategy for growing your fan base. KEY TAKEAWAYS Never pay for guaranteed streams: Legitimate playlist placement is never "bought" — any service promising guaranteed streams or virality for a fee is a red flag for bot activity and playlist scams. Watch your Spotify for Artists data: Sudden streaming spikes, unusual listener locations, or high streams-per-listener ratios can signal your music has been swept into a botted playlist without your knowledge. Vet curator profiles before trusting a playlist: Generic usernames, fake followers, and profiles mimicking official Spotify editorial branding are common signs of an inauthentic playlist. Use Spotify's own tools first: Pitching directly to Spotify editorial playlists, building your own Artist Playlists, and encouraging fans to playlist your music are all safer, more sustainable ways to grow streams than third-party promotion services. Playlists are an acquisition tool, not a growth strategy: Real fan connection (through live shows, email lists, and social media) is key to growing your music career. Playlists help get more ears on your music, but it’s up to you to retain new fans. 1. Use Spotify’s own playlist tools If you have a release coming up, pitch your music to Spotify’s editorial playlists. (Spotify recommends pitching four weeks out or more to maximize your chances of placement.) You can also create your own playlists — mixing your music with your favorite tracks from friends, influences, and comparable artists. Promote these playlists to your fans and add them to your Spotify artist profile as Artist Playlists to boost your streams. Lastly, encourage your fans to create playlists of their own with your music — gamify it by awarding a playlist that best captures your influence or fits a certain theme. 2. Do your research before using a playlist promotion service As a categorical rule, never use a service that guarantees streams in exchange for payment. In general, if a service sounds too good to be true, it isn’t legitimate. Here are some other signs a service is a scam or using botted traffic: No contactable human providing the service No real information about how the service promotes your music or examples of the playlists they use Unrealistic promises like virality or guaranteed streaming counts Cold or unsolicited outreach over emails or social media Requests for a “donation” or “fee” to keep your music on a playlist No signs of verified legitimacy from reputable sources (other artists, online reviews, etc.) 3. Monitor your streaming activity in Spotify for Artists Your music can get swept up in bot traffic without your consent — and you can still be penalized for it. That’s why it’s crucial to stay on top of your streaming data in Spotify for Artists and watch for suspicious activity. A few metrics worth monitoring closely: Top playlists: Treat any unexpected placement on a large playlist with caution. (More on how to evaluate playlist legitimacy in the next section.) Streams over time: An unexpected spike in listenership can signal a new playlist placement or bot activity. Drill down to see where those listeners are actually coming from and take stock of your own promo efforts — have you run ads or played major shows that could account for the spike? Listeners per location: Unexplained spikes in areas you haven’t been promoting are suspicious — particularly any low population areas with disproportionately high streaming numbers. Streams per listener: This can vary naturally — especially for new artists who might be encouraging their same inner circle to listen multiple times — but watch out for suspicious ratios (i.e. anything more than the casual 3-5 times per listener). 4. Investigate the playlists your music appears on Routinely check your top playlist placements in Spotify for Artists to verify the authenticity of the playlists and the curators. You can use this same criteria for checking the legitimacy of playlists that a third-party promo service uses as well, but be aware that even if everything seems to check out, these platforms still carry risks. If you suspect your music has been placed on a botted playlist, report it to Spotify. Here’s what to look out for at the playlist level: Curator profile: Look out for generic profiles with inauthentic profile photos, nonsense usernames, and approximately the same amount of saves on every playlist they own. Curator followers: Real accounts should have mostly real followers. If an account is generic and also has fake followers (nonsense usernames, no profile photos, and no user activity), steer clear. Playlist curation: Be wary of user-generated playlists that mimic the look of official editorial playlists — with a Spotify logo in the top left, the same Spotify font, and lifestyle imagery. They’re trying to mislead you. Also avoid playlists that don’t have any clear curational vision or coherency and a robotic or nonsense description. 5. Focus on real fan connection If you’re an emerging artist, build a solid foundation for your fans before you chase playlist placements. That means claiming and optimizing profiles across streaming and social platforms, planning a well-rounded release strategy, and doubling down on the channels where you connect best with fans — live performances, online forums, email newsletters, and social media. Streams you gain from a strong playlist placement won’t necessarily earn you loyal fans if you don’t have a strong strategy to retain new listeners. Treat playlists as an acquisition tool — not your entire playbook. If you do land on your dream playlist, make it count. When a curious new listener clicks through from the playlist to your profile — then to your social media — that’s your chance to make a strong first impression. That listener is looking to learn more about you, spot shared followers and similar artists, and see that you're active and serious about your music. All of that work lies beyond chasing playlists. The truth: Fan growth is hard work Playlists are attractive for fast and easy streaming growth, but never put your music at risk by employing a predatory service or by taking unexpected spikes in listenership at face value. Follow the tips in this blog to protect your music and focus on building systems to genuinely connect with fans. Building a strong foundation of die-hard fans will always be more valuable than amassing a transient audience through playlisting alone. content: The following post is an op-ed from CD Baby's SVP of Product Sean Hallarman. It originally appeared on the Downtown Music blog. I came back from this year’s Music Biz conference convinced there’s never been a better time to be an independent artist. Panel after panel, demo after demo, I witnessed an explosion of new technologies that didn’t exist just a few years ago. AI – with the right support from a human – that will master your record, generate the artwork, and create a suite of marketing assets. Platforms that offer direct ownership of the fan relationship, rather than reach rented from an algorithm. And the part that stayed with me is that these tools are reaching a bedroom artist and a major label’s marketing team at the same moment. Access has been flattened. That flattening is one of the best things to happen to independent music in years. But it comes with a quieter challenge: when an artist can suddenly do almost anything, where do they start? Imagine finishing your first recording and getting ready to release it to the world. All the years you spent getting to that moment focused on creating art, and now you’re ready to introduce it into culture. At face value, it may seem that releasing that music is as simple as posting to social media. But the moment you distribute, you’ve suddenly opened a business: rights to sort out, royalty splits to agree, marketing campaigns to plan, streaming data to analyze. You’re confronted with decisions that’ll have long-term effects that are hard to undo once set in place. And now, on top of all that, there’s a wall of platforms and tools, each more powerful than the one that preceded it. Any one of them might help, which is exactly what makes it so hard to know what to reach for first. That navigation problem is the part I keep coming back to, because as the entry point for independent artists to distribute their music, it’s increasingly our responsibility to solve. Even if it might make short-term commercial sense to bundle every capability an artist might eventually need into a single offering upfront, it doesn’t always serve artists. The better approach is to help them identify the right tool for the right moment in their development. Early on, it almost always comes down to the same thing: building connections with fans. The right tools make that easier. Analytics that show where a song is starting to resonate. Advertising that widens a circle already leaning in. Direct-to-fan tools that deepen the relationships worth keeping. But which of those actually fits at this stage depends on the artist. Some will love the data deep-dives, and others never will. Some come alive running a small, devoted community on a niche platform, and others don’t. That’s not a problem to solve. It’s just who they are. Connection only works when it’s authentic to the artist making it. The right tools don’t ask every artist to become the same kind of entrepreneur; they help each one lean into their own strengths at the right stage of their career. This is where music companies serving independent artists should act as guides, not just vendors. We’ve been thinking deeply about the standard we need to set for ourselves in serving DIY artists. The most exciting thing about this moment is not just that independent artists can now do most things a major label can do; it’s that they have more freedom than ever to decide what kind of career they want to build. We believe the measure of a useful platform is as much about helping them get their music heard as it is about helping them understand what matters now, what can wait, and what choices will protect their interests over the long term. It’s no longer enough to offer independent artists a bigger toolbox. We need to better serve them as a guide. content: Choosing your release date is about more than finding an open day on the calendar. Being strategic about timing can significantly boost your streams and help your release reach its full potential. The right date depends on several factors — from giving yourself and your fans enough lead time, to matching the sound and message of your music with the right moment. In this blog, we'll walk through the key considerations to help you land on the right date. KEY TAKEAWAYS Set your release date at least four weeks to prepare promo materials, platform profiles, and engage fans Fridays are the industry-standard release day, but earlier weekdays can help you stand out from the crowd Tying your release to a live show or other tentpole moment can drive early streams Consider holiday deadlines, eligibility windows, and press roundup timing Maintaining a consistent release cadence can help sustain momentum over time 1. Be proactive Set your release date at least four weeks in the future. That gives you time to gather promotional material, claim and set up platform profiles, and engage your fans. Ideally, choose your release date before or during the recording process to ensure you’re not scrambling to finalize details when you submit your music for distribution. 2. Release on Friday or go your own way From Spotify’s Release Radar (which refreshes every Friday morning) to press and blog Friday roundups, the music industry is built around Friday release days. Over 60 percent of releases CD Baby distributed in 2025 fell on a Friday. But independent artists have also seen success skipping the crowds on Friday to release in the earlier, quieter days of the week. Decide what’s best for you — but generally weekends get a bit lost in the mix. The next tip might help you narrow down your date further. 3. Line up your release date with a show or other tentpole moment Do you have an upcoming opening slot for a touring act, a release show booked, or a party planned? Consider setting your release date on a day that your fans will be engaged — that helps lock in some early streams and lets release day feel like the celebration you deserve. You can book a release show at a local venue, then set your release date for that day. 4. Be mindful of the time of year – holidays, seasons, cultural moments, deadlines, and more Releasing music at the right moment can amplify its impact, while poor timing can just as easily hold it back. Know your sound and how to describe it, then decide where it fits into the broader calendar. A love (or anti-love) song might do well around Valentine’s Day, a beachy, high-energy track might be best received in the summer, or a gloomy, weepy track might do best in colder months. Showing this intentionality in your releases makes them easier to market and more likely that your fans will listen. Ultimately, how you decide to leverage holidays, seasons, cultural moments and more is completely subjective. But here a few important deadlines to consider: GRAMMY Awards: If you’re interested in pursuing a GRAMMY nomination, ensure your release falls within the eligibility period. In 2026, that’s between August 31, 2025 and August 28, 2026. Distributor Holiday Deadlines: If you’re looking to release a holiday track (anywhere from November to early January), follow your distributor’s holiday deadline schedule. If you’re a CD Baby artist, keep an eye out for our 2026 deadlines, which we’ll announce in October. Industry Press Roundups: If you’re looking to be considered for industry press roundups (best of the week, month, year), it’s generally best practice to release music before editors are finalizing those lists. For a week, avoid Saturday and Sunday releases, for the month, avoid releasing on the final days of the month, and for the year, try to release by late November. These are of course, not hard and fast rules, but general guidance. 5. Find a release cadence that fits your audience Every artist’s fanbase is different, but having a release cadence (a standard amount of time between each release) can help keep your fans engaged. If you’re working your way up to an album, releasing singles every four to six weeks can help build momentum ahead of the full drop. You can use the waterfall release strategy to compound those streams, re-releasing previous singles with new tracks to gain incremental momentum, instead of just dropping the whole album in one go. Looking for more music industry trends? Check out our recaps of two cornerstone reports from 2025 — Luminate and IFPI’s Global Music Report — to get a confident grasp of topline industry stats and trends. 1. Fans are streaming more music than ever before Global on-demand audio streams hit 2.8 trillion in the first half of 2026, up 9.8% from the 2.5 trillion streams in the same period last year. What this means: Release your music to find your audience. Record-breaking streaming volume means more opportunities to build your fanbase. 2. Independent music distribution continues to grow Independently distributed tracks have grown across the mid- and lower-volume streaming tiers, demonstrating how independent sectors are carving out a sustainable ecosystem outside the mainstream. What this means: You don’t need a viral hit to lead a successful independent career. Focus on finding your niche audience, honing your brand as an artist, and leveraging the increasing array of marketing tools and services available to independent artists. 3. R&B/hip-hop declines slightly, while dance/electronic grows R&B/hip-hop slightly declined this year, losing a 1.6 share of points year-over-year. But make no mistake, the genre still dominates U.S. streams, accounting for about one in every four streams. Meanwhile, the dance/electronic genre saw the most growth (+18.9% year-over-year on-demand audio change). What this means: You can take shifts in genre listenership as encouragement to experiment with your sound, but don’t chase the trends or lose sight of your own artistic identity. 4. CD sales outpaced vinyl, but there’s more to the story CD sales grew 16%, outpacing vinyl sales that grew by a modest 2.4%. K-pop fans account for a significant share of this growth. So much so that excluding sales from BTS’ latest album ARIRANG and other K-pop sales, U.S. CD sales would have been up only 6.7% in the first half of 2026. But interestingly, only half of the Gen Z and Millennial CD buyers actually own a CD player, signalling the act of buying physical music is about aesthetic ownership and providing financial support to an artist as it is listening to the music on the medium itself. What this means: Don’t write off physical formats — or collectibles in general. Whether it’s actual physical releases (CDs, tapes, and vinyl) or standard merch items like shirts and stickers — give your fans a way to support you. 5. Rock music exemplifies the power of catalog music 75% of rock listening comes from tracks older than 60 months — what Luminate calls “deep catalog” listening. That’s in contrast to a genre like world music, where 34% of streams come from “current” tracks (0-18) months and another 26.5% come from tracks that are five years old or newer. What this means: No matter your genre, rock music proves you shouldn’t neglect your back catalog. Promote older tracks with the momentum you gain from new releases (e.g. “if you like the new track, listen to this one) and consider strategic re-releases and anniversary campaigns. content: “I don’t want to give up all the juice,” Michael Mwenso says, “but listen: the real key is you take all that stuff that you say is old, you mix it up, and then you get something new.” The belief that “nothing is old if you haven’t heard it before” is somewhat of a guiding principle for Michael. This month, we sat down with the artist, creator, curator, and educator to discuss his new single “Be Free,” his creative process, and advice he has for emerging artists. You can watch the full interview below or read on for key takeaways. About Mwenso Born in West Africa, Michael moved to London with his mother as a child. When his mother was deported to Nigeria, he found solace in Black music — listening to records, spending countless nights at Ronnie Scott’s Jazz Club, and eventually finding mentorship in great artists like James Brown. That early foundation set the direction for everything that followed. Wynton Marsalis invited him to join the programming team as curator at Jazz at Lincoln Center. There, he developed late night programming at Dizzy’s Club and networked with new musicians to start his group, Mwenso & The Shakes. With his creative collaborator, Jono Gasparro, he later co-founded Electric Root, which partners with institutions to decolonize music curricula with anti-racist, artist-led programming. And in 2022, he won an Emmy for Michael Mwenso Honors George Floyd, a documentary special that demonstrated his deeply held belief that art and activism are one. Mwenso’s new single, “Be Free” After more than a decade in the United States, Michael recently returned to London, and released his solo debut single “Be Free” — the first track off his upcoming album. Where much of his work to date has centered on collective language, the new single captures Michael taking on a more personal lyrical perspective and pushing his vocals to new heights. The single's release lined up with the Jon Batiste World Festival, a multi-night residency at Koko in London that Michael co-curated with Batiste. It was the perfect, organic platform for promoting “Be Free.” 3 lessons for independent artists from Mwenso Michael opened up about the people, values, and musical ideas that keep him inspired. The following three pieces of advice from our conversation stood out — lightly edited for brevity. 1. Love the music, but love the people first Michael has spent most of his life creating spaces, platforms, and events for artists to perform and connect with people. The secret to his success in curation? Loving people. He explained that every performance provides an opportunity for listeners to reconnect with the artists, experiences, and emotions that shape a musical lineage. Enabling that as a curator is a selfless and spiritual exercise, Michael notes, and a source of true joy. 2. Embody the qualities of successful artists Asked what it takes to succeed today, Michael pointed to three successful artists, each of whom exemplify characteristics he values: James Brown demonstrated focus and concentration, Wynton Marsalis showcases discipline, consistency, and practice, and Jon Batiste exemplifies foresight, calculation, and manifestation. 3. Nothing is old if you haven’t heard it yet Michael believes futuristic music comes from keeping the past alive and reinterpreting it. "Just because it's from nineteen-something doesn't mean you can't play it with fire and funk now," he said. In his framework, tradition pushes music forward, instead of holding it in place. What will you take from Mwenso’s story? Here are a few actionable tips based on what he shared: Build creative spaces (or support those who do) in your community for rehearsal, performance, networking, and inspiration Learn from your heroes — identify the characteristics that propelled their careers and seek to embody those in your work Break free of the shallowness of trends and the stuffiness of tradition – trace your inspirations back to their origins and aim to create something new from what you find Join over 2 million artists, like Mwenso Ready to make your statement? From gathering your assets for submission to promoting your music and growing your fan base, there's a lot of room to go wrong — even if it's not your first time. KEY TAKEAWAYS Over 100,000 tracks are released daily — a promotion plan is essential to stand out Cover art and metadata errors are a leading cause of release delays and rejections Most artists collect only one of six possible royalty types, leaving revenue unclaimed A consistent artist brand helps fans recognize and connect with you across every release Social media strategy should align with clear goals to avoid burnout Releasing music consistently builds momentum and makes fan growth easier to track 1. Submitting cover art or metadata that doesn't meet requirements Errors in your cover art or other metadata (i.e. essential information about your music) can lead to release delays and rejections. Before you submit your music, be sure your cover art meets platform requirements and your metadata is accurate and consistent. It’s not only about getting your release live on time. Clean and accurate metadata gives you a strong foundation for unlocking opportunities down the road — from arranging publishing deals to signing with a label. Good data makes everything easier. Releasing music without a plan to promote it to your fans Over 100,000 new tracks hit streaming platforms every day. That means just getting your music out there isn’t enough to find your fans. You need a plan to cut through the noise if you want to boost your streams. Resources to help: The 30-day release plan: Follow this detailed guide with a daily list of promo to-do’s Post-submission essentials: Learn what to do after submitting your music for distribution How to run a Spotify pre-save campaign: Launch a campaign to reach 100 pre-saves How to pitch Spotify editorial playlists: Get a 5-step template to craft an effective pitch How to reach 10,000 streams on Spotify: Learn tactics and strategies for reaching key streaming milestones from your first handful of streams up to 10,000 3. Missing out on revenue from uncollected music royalties Many independent artists release their music and focus solely on collecting recording royalties from streaming platforms through their distributor. But that’s only one of six common music royalties that together, add up to quite a bit of easy revenue. You’re probably earning other forms of royalties already — through streaming, live performances, radio play, and more. You just need to take the steps to collect them. Not building an artist brand that fans can identify No amount of marketing — be it paid ads, social posts, emails, or live shows — can make up for a lack of artist branding. Every appearance is a chance to make your identity and creative world stick with fans. But if your social profile has no consistent aesthetic, your live show feels different every time, and your releases don't tell a story, fans have no clear way to get to know you. Resources to help: Artist branding: Learn what an artist brand is and how to build one Networking: Get yourself out there and create opportunities How to get press coverage: Learn how to tell an impactful story behind your release How to write an artist bio: Learn how to write about yourself and your music How to create an electronic press kit: Impress journalists and media people with an EPK 5. Burning out on social media Social media enables you to reach global audiences in a matter of seconds. It’s also incredibly effective at making local music scenes more accessible and navigable. Maintaining your social media presence gives fans a way to discover your sound and stay connected with you — beyond the music. But make no mistake, burnout is real. If you feel overwhelmed or drained by constant posting, it’s time to reassess your strategy. Think: what do you want to accomplish and how will social media help you get there? Resources to help: Social media makeover: If your profiles are stale, this easy checklist helps with a refresh How to build an email list: Tired of algorithm chasing? See what email can do for you. Releasing music too infrequently to build momentum It’s difficult to grow your fan base if you aren’t releasing music on a consistent basis. Artists that don’t do either end up having to rebuild their foundation every time they start promoting a new release — and that’s not sustainable.
